their way into Cantigny, have been
repulsed, and at latest reports the
overseas men were holding their po-
sitions in the shell-torn village
strongly.

counter thrust late yesterday in an
effort| to regain the defences which
had been wrested from them in the
morning along two-kilometre front.
The enemy drive was preceded by a
heavy bombardment, which began at
. O'Clock in the afternoon. After
thirty minutes of artillery prepara-
tion the Germans advanced, but were
caught in an intense fire from the

forced to retire without having come
into close contact with the American
infantry.

WITH THE FRENCH ARMY IN
FRANCE, May 29.-The Germans
advanced against the French lines
again to-day after throwing further
masses of troops into the battle.
Both f1anks of the battle line were
the scene of very heavy fighting by
inferior numbers against superior,
with the result that the Allies were
obliged again to cede ground at sew
eral points.


Besides Won Boehm's and Won Be-
lows armies, many divisions of Won
Hutier's troops were engaged. These
specially trained units had partici-
pated in the first rush .on March 81
and had since then been reconsti-
tuted.


An enormous number Of light
machine guns were employed by the
Germans as well as a large fleet of
tanks and much heavy and light ar
tillery, while the German aviators
we're extremely active.


Officers Sacrifice Live


From the plain toward Juvincourt,
Ville-auBois, Pontavert and Berry
au-Bac, numerous tanks came into ac-
tion. For considerable time the thin
allied line held out, but as the enemy
debouched, wave after wave, the
French and British, almost submerged
fell back slowly, getting across the
river. Several British officers after
ward sacrificed their lives in destroy
ing the bridges.


Almost simultaneously overpowering
enemy forces made their way to the
top of the Chemin des Danes ridge
and also to the western end of this
road, in the neighborhood of Chavig-
non and Malmaison, and the troops
holding these points were obliged to
recede.


The allied movement to the rear
was executed with the greatest pre-
cision. There was no disorder and all
the units kept in constant liasion.


Readjustmcnt of Line Necessary


Further east other British divisions,
amalgamated with French colonial
troops, held fast. They are still firmly
sticking to their positions, although
they have been compelled to rearrange
part of their front in order to keep
alignment with their retiring COM
rades.


In the direction of Scissors read
justment Of the front line also became
necessary, in consequence of the fall
ing back of the centre, where the Ger
mans were pushing hardest


The fighting has been continuous for
two days through country composed
of a series of chalky plateaus, with
winding valleys, whose slopes are half
clothed with trees and contain many
caverns. Along the top of one of the
principal ridges runs the famous
Chemin des DANES, from which valleys
spread angularly toward the Aisne.
The Allied possession of this ridge
compromised the security of the Ger
man southern flank.


The encmy's torrent of divisions,
rolling forward. found only the thinnest
line of Allied troops facing the advance
These fell back before the irresistible
pressure. retiring, but struggling vail
antly. The torrent as it moved for
ward became even stronger, for the
Germans added new forces to it, Even
the Aisne did not stay its rush.


Follow Allies Across River


The Germans followed the Allies
across the river ard at the same time
spread along the sides, the Allies hav-
ing decided that it was useless to sac
rifice men in efforts to hold these po-
sitions with too few defenders.


The southern slopes of the Aisne Val |
ley offered good ground to the Allies to
stand, had they been in sufficient force. |
But the Germans were in immensely
superior numbers, and the Allied COM
chose to retire to the plateau
beyond, and thus give an opportunity
for the reserves to concentrate 1t is !
probable before the advancing German |
torrent weakens that further territory
will fall into the hands of the enemy. |
That, however, in the opinion of French |
officers, will not affect .he strength Of !
the Allied forces. which retain their
striking power for the future.


The French and British kept in the !
closest touch throughout the battle,
working together as a single unit. |

LONDON, Feb. 11.-"Violent engage
ments" in Flanders are reported in to-
DAYS official communique from Berlin,
and the enemy statement is borne out
in part by Field Marshal Hag. The
German report places the heaviest in
fantry activity near Warncton, on the
River Lys, and Armentieres, to the
south, but apparently the fighting
spread over nearly every part OF the
Ypres salient and southwark into the
Arras region.


The Australians conducted the most
successful action of the last two days
when they raided the enemy's trenches
south of Messines, on the southern end
of the Ypres salient, last night, killing
100 Germans, taking thirty-seven. others
prisoner and capturing three machine
guns and trench mortar. Seldom has
q raiding operation resulted more sue
cessfully. Following the action the
Germans delivered sharp counter at
tack, but were easily repulsed, accord
ing to Haig's report tonight, the Brit
ish suffering twenty casualties.


Australian troops left the trenches
last night and penetrated the Ger
man lines southeast of Messines, on the
southern end of the Ypres front, Haig
reports, inficting severe casualties on
the enemy and bringing back twenty
eight prisoners. The Germans claim
the capture of prisoners in forefeld en-
counters cast of Ypres.

lines with shell, the Crown Prince sent

Greater New York's seaside theatrical
activity is scheduled for resumption on
Monday afternoon, May 27, when the
New Brighton Theatre, at Ocean Park
way, Brighton Beach, inaugurates its
tenth regular season.


George Robinson, general manager,
under whose direction the oceanside
playhouse has enjoyed its greatest
period of popularity, promises for the
coming summer a rigid adherence to
the major vaudeville policy adopted
when the theatre was first opened, and
to which it has been successfully and
exclusively devoted ever since.


Visitors to the seashore will find the
theatre undisturbed by the big fire that
threatened to devastate Coney Island
last Thanksgiving Day. 1t was gener-
ally conceded at the time that the un-
relenting brick walls of the playhouse
checked the blaze and saved the island.

The only official details were con-

"The Navy Department is informed

Had the shell exploded after entering

PARIS, Dec. IA (By The Associ-
ated Press).-This is a greater night
IN Paris than armistice night. The
city is ablaze with Examinations, the
boulevards are thronged with
crowds, dancing and singing and

Concorde has been turned into a
great dancing pavilion, where Amer
lean soldiers are favorite partners.
America is the predominating word.


President and Mrs. Wilson made

greeted by two million persons, we'll
nigh half the population not only of
the city but of the surrounding dis
tricts. They were attended by Pres
ident Poincare, Premier Clemenceau
and others among the most eminent
figures of France. Flowers were
dropped around their carriage, air
planes winged overhead, guns
sounded.


All Classes Pay Honor


But observers were impressed with
something more than the magnitude
and beauty of the reception-by some
quality Of warmth that made it diff
ferent from the visits to Paris re-
Gently made by the sovereigns of the
Allied nations.


The imagination and interest of
France have been stirred by the
President of the United States as
by no other leader beyond the bor-
ders. All classes and parties in this
country have united to pay honor
to the United States through it's
President. They greet him as the
representative Of ideals now dawn
ing upon Europe.


In the eyes of the immense
crowd welcoming him." says the
Temps" president Wilson repre-
sents two invincible forces-the
material force which permitted the
war to be won, and also the force
which will sanctify peace"

Thirty-six thousand soldiers, the
flower of the French army, lined
the avenues from Dauphine Gate to
the Murat Mansion, which during
their stay in Paris will be the home
Of the President and his wife. AL
pine chasseurs and zouaves, fresh
from the battlefield of Champagne,
and colonial troops, from whose
uniforms the mud of the Somme
had only few days ago been re-
moved, occupied the post of honor.


They gently, but firmly, /kept
order among the enormous crowds,
which ever pressed forward in
eagerness to have a closer look at
the guests of France.

enceau and other French officials

railway station, together with
French and American military Of
ficers and prominent civilians, while
the Republican guard band, called
out in his honor, greeted him with
the strains of "The ar-Spangled
Banner"


Bares His Head to Throngs


After the presentations and other
formalities of welcome had been con-
cluded, the President, with Mrs.
Wilson and the other members of the
party, entered open carriages of state
and drove under overcast skies along
the appointed route, escorted by the
mounted Republican Guard between
solid ranks of French troops.


The route was lined for miles with
captured guns and other battle tro.
phies, and every available space was
crowded by vast crowds waving and
shouting their welcome-such crowds
as have rarely been seen in Paris.


President Wilson was constantly
barring his head and smiling upon
the throngs in acknowledging hi.

CHICAGO, May 26-Memories Of
the olden days when the rivalry be-
tween the Giants and Cubs was at it's
height were revived here this after
noon, when twenty-five thousand wildly
cheering fans saw the home team de-
feat the league leaders for the second
day in succession. The score was 5
to /.


The crowd not only filled all the
seats, but there was fringe of the
rabid encircling the playing field, and
hundreds more, including many women,
peeked at the play from the opening
under the grandstand. There is not
the slightest doubt that Chicago is very
much in favor of Sunday ball.


Two bands, one the escort of the
ment from Sousa's band at the Great
Lakes training station, supplied music
in bountiful portions before the game
and between the innings. The two
organizations Joined in leading the
singing of the "Star- Spangled Banner"
at the opening of the seventh frame
and the thousands of throats set the
air quiverng.


Jim Vaughn on Mound


Big Jim Vaughn was selected by
Manager Mitchell to do the finging for
the Cubs and the Giants as ever found
Jim's slants far from their liking
Only four hits did they get and two Of
these came in the first inning, before
Vaughn was really ready for business.


Slim Sallee, the New York pitcher,
had quite a different experience. The
Cubs fairly murdered everything he
chose to serve to them and collected q
total of thirteen safe blows, including
4l ~ -
hits also were for two bases.


The Giants made their only run in
the first inning. Ross Young singled
to center and advanced to third while
Zeider was tossing out Benmy Kauff.
George Burns struck out, but Heinie
Zimmerman answered the booes and
jeers of his friends by singing to CEN
ire, tallying Young. Heinie aroused
further recognition from fans and
bands by stealing second, but Fletcher
was unable to do more than give
Vaughn a close play at first on
Arthur's grounder to Merkle.


The Cubs did not get very familiar
with Sallee's shoots until the third
inning, when they banged out double
and two singles for the run that tied
the score. It looked like a real ball
game and the fans settled back in their
seats, those who had seats, expecting a
pitchers duel, with runs few and far
between. But it turned out otherwise,
much to their delight.


Settled in the Fifth


The fifth inning settled the outcome,
the Cubs going on a slugging rampage
that netted them three runs. Killifer
opened the pot with double to left
field. and Jim Vaughn followed with a
single to the same territory that put
Killifer on third. Flanck was tossed
out by Fletcher, but Hollocher brought
the crowd to it's myriad feet by sim
Cling to right field Killifer counting.
Young fumbled the ball bit and then
hesitated so long about throwing home
that Vaughn pursued his battery mate
over the plate. Mann added to Sallee's
agony by drawing a base on balls after
Hollocher had stolen second. Merkle
forced Hollocher at third. Paskert
smashed the ball to right field for two
bases and Mann scored. That was all
for the time being, but it was more
than enough.


The Cubs went after Sallee again in
the seventh and put over the final run
of the game. With one out, Mann and
Merkle singled. Sallee made a wild
pitch and Mann registered on Holke's
catch of Paskert's long foul to right
field. 1t was fine play on the part of
Holke, who probably figured that he
would have plenty of time to nab
Mann.

CAMBRIDGE, Mass, May 25.--Yale
and Harvard divided honors in their
preliminary regatta on the Charles
River to-day. Harvard's freshmen, con-
querors of the Princeton first year
men, led the Yale freshmen crew all
the way over the mile and seven
eighths course, winning by length
and half. Harvard was timed at 10
minutes and seconds, and Yale at 10
minutes and Is seconds.


The contest between the second var
slty elghts was a gruelling fight to the
drop of the flag, the heavier Yale crew
having the stamina to lift their shell
across the line in the lead by half a
length. They caught the flag in 0:02,
with Harvard's time 10:04, considered
last for the rough water. The visitors
used Harvard boats.


In the freshman race the Harvard
youngsters ran away at the start until
half way over the course they had a
patch of open water over the Yale
boat. Here Yale made great rally
and closed the distance, but Harvard
was much smoother in the rought water
below the Harvard bridge.


In trying to row down the Crimson.
Yale began to splash and twice there
were bad breaks in the boat, enabling
Harvard to surge ahead. But each
time that Yale seemed hopelessly dis
tanced Captain Carson, in the cox
swain's seat, rallied his men and held
Harvards lead to length and a half.

son will enjoy something of the spirit

spent in the battle zone. 1t became

chases and looking about without
being recognized.

BY the associated Press.


WITH THE AMERICAN ARMY ON THE
LORRAINE FRONT, Sept. 14.-Aside from
the strategic value OF tho reduction of
the st. Mihlsl salient. the operation by
tho Americans has Melted vast numbers
OF prisoners and huge quantities of
guns, ammunition and general stores.


Tho desperate efforts of the enemy
to escape through the forest near Wig
neulles partly succeeded, but not so
well as to detract from the brilliant re-
suit. Before the American line stretched
across the edge of the woods frightened
1t is estimated that thousands escaped
from the trap. Those who did escape
were small units, rarely greater than
companies. and never offered to fight
unless encountered by some patrol, and
even then their resistance was slight.


The spirit of retreat had entered that
part of the German army, and there
were scores of instances where the men.
and even officers protested satisfaction
at their capture.


Gas Projectors Captured.


Among the war materials captured
was a long train of freight cars con-
tanning complete equipment Of gas pro-
5ectors, and this may have had bear





carry out a gas attack shorty before
the Americans began their operation. 1t
Is known that the Germans planned such
an attack at one point, but a prisoner
said that the equipment was delayed and
1t was decided to postpone the attack.


When the st. Nthiel operation began
there were from 10000 to 100000 Ger
mans inside the salient. They escaped
at the rate of 1000 hourly. but the
pincers closed and trapped hitherto
unknown number. The 1890 already
counted prisoners does not include the
bulk Of those believed to be trapped in
che salient.


The enemy counter attacked against
part of the American lines Friday eve
ming and again during the night, but
met with an intense and accurate artil-
1ery fire and recoiled. The Americans
took few prisoners in these attacks.
Some Hard Fighting Occurred.
Hari' fighting has taken place in the
quarries northeast OF Tey-en-H aye
where the Germans had placed one big
gun and many machine guns in IA well
defended position. Additional Austrian
prisoners have been taken. Naive
civilians said they came in only few
days ago.


ARTILLERY fire and gas shells were
sent against certain American positions
during the night, but they did little
damage.


The Americans are organizing their
newly taken positions rapidly and are
pushing forward exploitation parties.
Prisoners lid supplies are being COL
aected. and roads are being instructed
in No Mans Land. Much booty and
ammunition have fallen to the Franco
American allies.


Prisoners and refugees alike are
great y impressed by the fact that the
Americans are eating white bread. re-
garding it as a particularly ominous
sign for Germany.


Throughout the night and early<to day
Pershing's men continued to advance
and finished clean'ng-up the st. Mihel
salient. They c,edied the forests of Turk
ing Germans.


Artillery Was in Retreat.


PRISONERS make conflicting statements
respecting German preparedness for an
attack In this sector. Some say it was
unexpected. others declare they had nd
vance information of the hour and place
of the attack. Still others expected it
would take place on the 18th and say
that the artillery had been ordered to
withdraw OIL the night of the attack.
The posts command was being moved
when the attack began and therefore
was caught unawares in the barrage.
This apparently explains the light coun-
ter artillery fire Thursday morning.


A German prisoner officer is quoted
ms saying: 1.-The Hindenburg line in
Its present state is untenable."


Thirty-six hours OF fighting netted
Gen. Pershing's forces approximately
1855 square miles of territory in the
st. Mihiel salient which had been in
German hands since the autumn of
1914


Following the American troops
through the captured villages the As
ISOLATED Press found on every hand evil
dences of long control by the Germans.
Bills for electric lighting and supplies
had been paid with curious currency. on
which the Germans had printed French
monetary terms.


Inhabitants Were Isolated.


The inha bitants of the salient were abb
soluteiy ignorant of the events OF his
tory in the past four years. knowing
only what their captors had told them.
Here the sad stories heard In the whole
of the reclaimed districts of France
were accentuated by the long years OF
German control which had isolated the
people from news of relatives and of
world happenings.


Every American entering the villages
experienced the same reception as that
accorded to Secretary of War Baker and
Gen. Pershing and their party. Aged
men and women seized and kissed the
hands Of the officers and correspondents,
crying and laughing. the curiously aged
children initiating their elders unknow-
tngly.


For their own compatriots, however,
the greeting was deeper, and the French
patrols and troops following were even
more affected than those who had been
delivered.


Later in the evening Gen. Pershng
and Secretary Baker resumed their
tourney in other sections of the regained

der in uniform grinding out Christ

FORCES ON THE MARINE, June
17.-The Germans to-day began
using gas to n greater extent along
this front than they have done here
tofore. Belleau Wood came in for
its share, but despite the heavy GAS
and other shelling the American
lines remain intact.


An American patrol crossed the
Marne last night, east of Chateau
Thierry, and at once established con-
tact with the Germans. After an
exchange of shots the Americans re-
crossed the river safely by means of
boats.


The American forces along the
south bank Of the Marne are con-
stantly crossing to the north side,
where the enemy is intrenched in
wooded low lands, returning safely.
Most of the American patrols have
crossed by boat; others, singly or
in small numbers, swim the stream,
which is about 15O feet wide.


Twice only recently have the
larger patrols encountered the
enemy. 1t is known, however, that
some Of Germany's best troops are
facing the Americans here.


Guns Increase Activity


The enemy artillery fire in the Sec
ton east of Chateau Thierry has
been increasing fog some time, and
the American fire has increased pro-
portionately.


The Germans last night started to
construct a foot bridge across the
Marne at this point, but were discov-
cred, and abandoned the attempt
even before the American machine
gunners on the bank could get into
action.


To the west the Germans have
taken to drenching certain localities
with mustard gas. One of these
places is Belleau Wood, the Germans
apparently thinking that this was
the only way to drive the American
troops out. But it was not, for they
are still holding all their positions,
and at the same time are giving the
enemy some clouds of American gas
to worry about.

The Austrians on the third day of
their offensive yesterday again failed
in their attempt to drive forward
along the Italian battlefront.


On the middle Piave, the centre of
the active fighting line, and on the
lower Piave, they have made slight
gains at heavy cost. On the inn
portant northern mountain front
they have suffered such serious re-
verses that they have had TO reor-
ganize their forces.


Italians Fall Back Slowly


Throwing the greatest weight
against the Italian line on the Mon
tello Plateau, high ground on the
middle Piave and the key to the
Venetian Plains, the Austrians
pushed a short distance west and
south. The Italians, falling back
slowly before superior numbers, held
their line on the crest of the heights
running east from Ciano.


On the Asiago Plateau, on the
mountain front, terrific British coun-
ter attacks have thrown the enemy
back and completely reestablished
the original line.


Capo Sile Occupied


Following up their early minor
successes on the lower Piave. the
Austrians pressed their attacks with
renewed vigor, but met growing Itai-
ian resistance. They advanced short
distances west of the river near Mu-
sile and st. Andrea. Further south
the Austrians occupied Capo Sile on
the border of the swamp region.


Two thousand additional prisoners
on the Piave front are claimed BY
Vienna, bringing the toll on that
side of the "L" front to 1900, and
the total for the whole drive to 49,
600. Nearly 5000 prisoners have
been taken by the Allied armies.

WASHINGTON, May 26.-Athletic
sports have become So popular among
the American soldiers training in the
United States that the Commission on
training camp activities has found it
necessary to extend it's work along all
lines, and in some camps so many men
are reporting for play when free from
duty that it has been found necessary
to enlarge the athletic fields.


A summary of camp recreation is
sued to-day by the commission shows
that baseball is the most popular
sport. To encourage play full equip
ment has been sent to all camps, in
cluding more than 10000 balls and
5000 bats, while new diamonds have
been laid out in nearly every training
centre. Camp Lewis, Washington, is
using sixteen fields. Battalion, regi-
mental and r-regimental leagues
have been formed and it is planned to
have the camp champions meet in the
fall in post games wherever
possible.


Next to the national game, boxing
is proving the most popular recreation.
More than 5000 sets of gloves have
been sent to the men and so great has
become the demand for instruction
that in one camp alone more than 800
assistant instructors are kept busy.


Track athletics, golf, swimming, ten
mis- and polo have many followers.
while Sports which are proving popu-
lar include volley ball, push ball and
'cross--country running.

After rowing in the "pollywog" ad-

ming pool for the last five days, Coach

yesterday to send his men up and down
the Hudson, with most favorable
weather conditions existing.

favor to-day, and if the same results

Carnegie Lake in the highest of spir-
it's


Getting away under a heavy, accu-
rate stroke that made the coach speak
words of encouragement, the varsity
eight pulled Upstream for almost a
mile. Then Rice signalled for Neale,
the coXswain, to turn around and get
ready to drive the crew downstream
for three good miles.


Plotting his launch just astern of
the varsity she'll, the final directions
were given and the pistol was heard.
With the accuracy and speed that have
marked many Poughkeepsie regatta
the Blue and White varsity crew
pulled away. The pace continued until
within about half mile of the finish
Then Rice instructed his men to go
the limit. They did, and, to the sur
prise of the coach, every one emerged
from the trial spin showing but very
little effect from the first real grind
of the season.


After the days trial spins, with the
juniors and freshmen coming in for
their share of workouts, the Blue and
White instructor admitted that he was
more impressed with the showing made
by the varsity than at any time dur
ing the season. He intimated that, if
there were to be signs of weakening,
yesterdays sprint by the first shell men
would have developed them. And, as
the results came forth, noticeable ex
pressions of astonishment were visible
on the part of the crew authority.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 12.-While no
specific complaint has reached Major
General Ireland, surgeon general of
the army, that soldiers in hospitals in
this country had not been paid
promptly, Secretary Baker believes it
possible that there are many of the
wounded and sick soldiers brought
home from France who probably have
not received their pay for several
months.


The Secretary explained that the
old pay system under which company
commanders made out pay rolls for
all the men on their company rosters
had broken down because wounded and
sick men became SO far separated from
their commands that it was impossible
for the company commanders to know
what had become Of them.


To Offset this a new system of indi-
vidual pay books was inaugurated, Mr.
Baker said, but because of the great
size of the force in France, it has not
been brought into complete operation.


The War Secretary said that on his
return from France recently, he issued
instructions that no men be embarked
from France, except with complete out
fits of clothing and with enough money
to provide them with funds for Incl
dental needs on the journey and for
some time at the hospitals in this
country.

WITH THE AMERICAN ARMY IN
FRANCE. January 12.-The American
mother Of young soldier buried behind
will receive letter from a French count
ess. consoling her with the assurance tina.
the tears Of an American woman fell at
the graveside even in that far-off war
swept zone. This touch Of sentiment
softened the ot6cial report of a sad oc-
currence when Regular Army engineer
ing detachment, which had been in the
trenches more than a month, returned to
the training area. Countess de Buyer
Mimeure. former American girl, famous
for her work in rebuilding devastated viii
lagos near the front and who married a
Fench general, was the good angel who
gave the softening effect of woman's
presence Mt grim military funeral under
winter skies and with German guns BOOM
ing in the distance.


The countess was making holiday pill
grimage through the villages near the
lighting zone, which is barred from the
outside world as effectively as desert
island. distributing presents to the chill
dren living in these desolate surroundings.
When she arrived at the village where
the engineers were billeted she left the
gayety to take part in the funeral, which
she learned was in progress, and then
promised to write to the mother of the
dead soldier


Countess de Buyer Mimeure is closely
associated with Ethel Crocker of San
Francisco, sister Of Princess Poniatow-
sky. IN work in the dangerous war areas,
where few civilians and women rarely are
permitted to enter. Not far from Troyes,
a residence city near the front, the en-
gineers were engaged at night In building
a new first line trench in advance Of the
trench destroyed by the German barrage
on the night the enemy raided the Ameri-
can lines in November After the first
night the fresh earth on the white snow
disclosed the work they had been doing,
and when the engineers returned the sec
ond night the German artillery broke
loose, killing one and wounding another
The others grabbed their rifles and ran
forward to assist a French patrol in re-
pelling the expected raid. No German
patrols appeared and the barrage stopped.
The men returned and worked two hours
to prove that they were not panic stricken.
When they left they carried their dead
and wounded with them.


Christmas day was unlucky for the en-
gineers, for though the turkeys arrived
the men had only one stove and green
wood to cook with, and that was not
enough. They ate canned beef instead
Most of the time they were working in
had a two hours hike on the snow each
way between the front and their billet.
They made the march back to camp in
two hours. The men are in excellent con-
dition. considering the hardships they
have experienced.

yesterday the enemy began harass-

Denser Masses Than Ever

rules IF open warfare.


1t must be considered that repuls-
ing mass attacks on what is known
in trench warfare as the first line
is impossible. The first lines in this
new open fighting are merely a
series of advance posts and small or
ganized position of defence, which
the enemy must overcome before
reaching the real line of resistance
further back.


At the moment yesterday morn

tinued an intermittent shelling of

BRUSSELS, Dec. 23.-1t is reported
here that Holland has been informed by
Great Britain of her intention to send
supplies to the British army of occupa-
ton in Germany by way of the river
Scheldt and Dutch Limburg


The Scheldt River was source of con-
troversy between Holland and the Allies
throughout the war, particularly at the
time when Germany was using the
Scheldt and other Dutch waterways for
transporting war materials into Bel
GUM.


The Scheldt flows through three
countries, France. Belgium and Hol-
land. 1t rises in France, in the depart
ment of the Aisne and flows first north,
into Belgium, then northeast to Ant
werp. north of which it spreads out
into the large branching estuary which
merges with the Rhine Delta and opens
by several wide channels into the
North Sea, through southwestern Hol-
land


Last year the British government
stopped all commercial cable communi-
cation with Holland until the Dutch
government halted the transportation
of German war material over the
Scheldt into Belgium.

killed in the wreck on the New York

this afternoon, according to a report
received at the railroads head offices
here.


All the persons injured were on the
Empire State Express. which left New
York this morning for Buffalo.


Derailed freight cars had blocked the
tracks on which the Empire was run
ming. The engine, combination bag
gage and smoker, and a coach were
derailed when this train ran into the
wreckage, and were thrown across the
eastbound tracks into the path of No,

was derailed. All the cars of No. 16

LONDON, April s.-Jerusalem's nrst
Easter since the British occupation was
celebrated with quiet solemnity. says
Reuters correspondent in the Holy
City. SThe usual swarms Of pilgrims


who throng Jerusalem at this season
were missing. naturally. but their
place was taken to some extent by


khaki-clad figures who participated In
the services Of both the Protestant and
Catholic churches.


"Pontifical mass" the correspondent

by the governor of Jerusalem and
numerous officers including repre-
The Passover coincided with our
festival and was celebrated with a
new meaning of Joy for the Jews in
the occupied territory.


Big Change in Four Months.
Although occupation only dates
four months back, the very atmosphere
of this region seemed to have under
gone a change. Distress has vanished
and sickness and fear no longer are
at the thresholds of the towns and
villages Everywhere there is evidence
of reviving industry and prosperity.
What has contributed more than any
thing else to immediate relief has been
the employment OF thousands OF natives
upon the repair Of roads.


Entire households work together In


little groups breaking stone and draw


ing fair wages which are paid regu-


larly. The roads in the neighborhood


Of the bigger towns are lined sometimes


for miles with busy laborers. Christian
Moslem and Jew: men, women and chill
dren. Road-making and repairing pro-
vides an occupation for all who are
able to work.


Everybody realizes that new era
has dawned for their land. The Beduoins
can graze their hocks In peace and Sc
curity and husbandmen can till the
soil with the knowledge that they will
not be robbed of the fruits of their
labor. The roads which are being built
solidly in every direction and the rail-
way to Egypt will insure them easy dis
posal of their surplus yield, and the
means of satisfying their wants as re-
CARDS imports from abroad.


The benefits of rule of liberty and
Justice already are making themselves
felt. and the people are beginning to
feel a lively gratitude to the British
soldier who moves in their midst show
ing them nothing but kindness, fairness
and good nature"

LONDON. Jan. 16.-Bitter fighting

in several weeks. From the Asiago
Plateau to the heights of Valdobbia
dene assaults and counter assaults,
bursts of artillery fire and patrol en-

and Vienna War Offices claim tonight

ground along the mountain front.


On the delta of the Piave the fighting
was at times extremely violent also

attacks against the Italian positions
east of Capo Sile, but meeting with
failure.

ing the day, to the west of Col del

had unsettled Egypt's brains showed
signs of abatement.


The intelligence of the people became

istic.

tasks. The. grain shot forth again; the
roads recovered their animation; the
ports saw again fleets of heavily laden
vessels; the wor.bs of the women became
fruitful again.


The verbal intoxication that had rem.
dered the Egyptians incapable of any
organized and sustained effort vanished
with the echo of the last speeches.


Egypt was then seen driving the in
cendiary and murderous barbarians into
the desert, where they almost all per-
lshed, and, this plague being cured, all
others gave way in their turn.


Once more the Egyptians had given
proof of wisdom after having suffered
from the most hideous of follies.

daylight Sunday. Reveille was sounded
shortly after o'clock, the Americans
had breakfast by and the march began
soon afterward.


but during the afternoon the sun broke
through the haze for brief periods, but
hardly long enough to relieve the dismal
atmosphere Of the German villages
through which the Americans passed.


The advance of the American army OF
occupation into Germany was held up
BY the limited number of bridges across
the Sauer and Moselle rivers. The prin-
cipal bridges used were those at Echter-
mach, .Rosport and Wasserbillig, on the
Sauer. and Grevermacher, Wormeldange
and Remich, on the Moselle. Several
small bridges and fords between these
villages were utilized by various units


The American divisions marched with
full war equipment of steel helmet, gas
mask, rife sand belts filled with car
tridges. The heavy artillery also rum
bled along the German roads. while the
ammunition wagons kept step with the
troops.


The main roads encountered during
the first days march into Germany were
in good condition.


There were no flags or other decora-
tions in any Of the towns through which
the Americans marched and no music
except that furnished by the Americans.
wherever the Americans asked Ques-
courteous replies. In the restaurants
and stores the Germans sold to the

wartime prices.

North and south of the Somme the

ground. In the former region they
have evacuated their positions over
five-mile front to the British north
of Albert, while in the latter they
have been beaten back in the hilly
and wooded district just north OF the
Oise river by the French.


German front line trenches at Beau
mont Hamel, Serre, PuisieuXauMo
and Bucquoy have been found unten-
able by the enemy in the face of the
recent activity by the British along
the line from Albert to Arras, while
the French have persevered in their
violent attacks against the Germans
on the sector which dominates the
lower portion of the Picardy plain and
the Disc valley, and have encroached
further upon the Lassigny massif and
the Thiescourt plateau, and farther
south have captured the important
town of Ribecourt.

and of all the German positions be-

have been centered.

Germans foresee the ultimate success

retrograde movement seemingly indi-

The fighting in Picardy recalls the
great offensive carried out there by
the British and French in 1916, and
the German strategic retreat" to the
Hindenburg line IN February and
March, 1917.


The British had forced their way
during the fall eastward from Albert
to the neighborhood of Grand Court.
west of Bapaume, and the French
were before Noyon, almost directly to
the south, when. in the early months
of 1917, the Germans discovered that
the allies had massed guns and ma
.erials for a major offensive. They
then retreated to the Cam mbrai-La Fere
line, which they occupied until March
81. 1918, and from which they launch
ed their first great offensive of the
present summer.


The field over which the British are
fighting today is familiar ground to
them, but to the south the French
must force the enemy back from terri
tory newly occupied during the March
offensive. Six miles to the eastward
they will come to the old battle-
ground of Picardy.

TORONTO, Ont, Nov. 3O-For the
second time in two weeks, Bethlehem
the soccer champion of the United
States, to-day defeated a specially Sc


ected team from all the talent which
Toronto, the Queen City of Canada, has
at it's disposal. The score was 2 to O.


There was record attendance for a
soccer crowd in Canada, and notwith-
standing that the weather conditions
were anything but favorable. 1t was
rain that spoiled the first game at
Newark a week ago Sunday, but it was
snow that marred the second contest
at Toronto


The Bethlehem team showed some
change from that which won the New
ark game, Ratican playing for Easton
at centre forward, Butler appearing at
inside right and Pepper going to left
field. The Toronto side had several
changes, including two new backs, and
altogether, was considered a stronger
aggregation than played at Harrison
Field.


The game was fraught with great
excitement at the start the Canadians

was, however, able to negotiate all the
shots that were sent to him, although
one gave him some trouble

dent that the Bethlehem lot were re-
serving their energies until the second
half. The visitors relied on their de-
fence being able to keep their goal
intact. and at periods the forwards
made brilliant dashes for the opposing
goal.


When the interval arrived without
any scoring the verdict was that the
teams had under the bad ground con-
dltlons put up Il splendid display. The
second half was quite different, for
during the whole forty-6ve minutes

rerior lot. and their play delighted the
onlookers. 1t was some time, however,

when the ice was broken it was we'll

NEW HAVEN, June 1.-The Harvard
varsity crew defeated the Yale eight
by length of open water in a two
mile race on the Housatonic River
above Derby. near here, late this after
noon IN a wartime substitute for the
annual dual regatta usually rowed at
New London. The time Of the winning
combination was 10 minutes and So
seconds. while Yale finished in IL min
utes and seconds.


The Crimson oarsmen took the lead
early in the race and were never
headed. although Yale made gallant
squirt near the finish and managed to
cut down portion Of the intervening
space. When the Blue blades of the
local university began to become
threatening. however, the Cambridge
crew lifted its beat to +hirty-four
strokes to the minute and quickly
pulled away again. finishing strongly
and with speed and endurance to spare


Rowed in Dead Water


The race was not particularly fast,
the contest being rowed in dead water
without current and under most try
ing weather conditions. A high tenn
perature and heavy, humid atmos phere
took early toll from the oarsmen, and
two of the Yale crew collapsed as the
she'll slid across the finish line.


Both in rowing form and power the
Harvard eight showed superior to the
Yale sweep swingers There was
greater unison in the blade work of
the Cambridge men, and they drove
their craft through the water without
perceptible drag between strokes. The
Yale shell failed to run smoothly be-
tween beats, and there were several
occasions when. in an effort to lift
the stroke, slight splashing developed.


Twenty Thousand Witness Race


Regardless of the absence of the
usual observation train, more than 20,-
600 spectators witnessed the race The
river edge on both shores for dis
tance of fully a mile above the finish
was lined with canoes, while the roads
were massed with parked motor cars.


The finish stakes were set close un-
der the high banks of the public park
of Shelton, and these bluffs were SOL
idly carpeted with spectators, while
across the stream, on the Derby side
OF the Housatonic, there were similar
groupings, including a large delegation
of Yale students in Naval Reserve and
army training corps uniforms.

LONDON. July 5.-The Italians are
continuing their pressure on the Aus
trians in the delta of the Piave and
have driven them back still further
along the eightmile front, the War
Office in Rome announced to-day At
several points between the Piave fork
and the Adriatic Sea the Italians have
pierced the Austrian lines and reached
the main channel of the river They
have captured 419 additional prisoners.


On the northern mountain front the
Allied armies have held their advan-
tage over the Austrians, blocking three
desperate enemy counter attacks near
Monte Grappa and on the Asiago plat
eau, which resulted in hand to hand
fighting, but everywhere holding their
own.


Northeast of Monte Grappa the Ital-
ans penetrated the Austrian positions
at the head of the Calcino Valley and
strengthened their hold on the Porte di
Salton heights. Thirty Austrians were
taken prisoner there.


There has been sharp artillery fight
ing on the mountain front. Severe
losses have been inflicted on the enemy,
the Italian War Office stated.

Fourth there was greater activity to-
day on the Toul front. The American
artillery shelled the. enemy heavily
with gas projectiles this morning, and
the Germans carried out their usual
bombardment of the front line and back
areas. Along the line there was con-
siderable rife firing

eral recommending and photographing
expeditions and drove off hostile ma
chimes which attacked them. One re-
connoitring plane gave battle to two

can returned safely.

to no purpose. The enemy patrols
were put to flight and raiding party
was driven off before it could reach
the American line.

The Holy Cross baseball team, with
Gill in the box, continued its winning
streak yesterday afternoon by trounc-
ing Columbia, 10 to l, on South Field
A home run and three-bagger by
O'Neill in the fifth and sixth innings,
respectively, driving in several runs
each time, combined with the fine twirl
ing of Gill, were entirely too much for
the local collegians.


For four innings Tommy Farrell,
Columbia's premier pitcher, held the
Holy Cross nine to one hit and one run,
made by Bowen, the centre fielder In
the fifth inning Farrell went to pieces
and passed five men. O'NeilI came to
bat with two on bases and knocked a
clean home run far out in centre field,
bringing in the three runs which
started the end for Columbia Dona-
hue, the Holy Cross shortstop, con-
tinued the pace and brought in Maloney
on two-bagger, scoring the fourth
run.


Columbia Pitchers Weak


The only branch of the game in
which Holy Cross especially outshone
the Morningside nine was in pitching.
Gill remained strong through nine in
nings, while Columbia's pitchers were
being hit right and left. Coach Coax
ley switched Johnny Hauck from third
base to the pitchers box in the sixth,
but the opposing batters were flushed
with victory, and knocked in three runs
in the sixth and two in the seventh.


Herb Koenig, who had been held
out because of an injury to his leg,
was tried and held the Holy Cross
batters down in the last two innings.
Off. his delivery they failed to get more
than d double, which was safely stop
ped on third.


The strong section of the Holy Cross
batting order with ONell, Bowen,
Maloney and Donahue formed more
dangerous combination than the hard
hitting infield of Columbia could mus
ter. Gill allowed only two hits in the
whole game.

cent of local boards quota were re-
turned home after reaching camp.

that much of the trouble is due to the
f1eXibility of the eligibility rules. Before

for eligibles was siXty-one inches. with
weight to correspond.


After these men reached the camp, he

height minimum made sixty-three inches,
with corresponding change In weight.
and consequently many sent away were
rejected by the military examiners.

use greater care in selecting the men

METZ FRONT. Sept. 22.-The Ger

American plans for the immediate

This state OF mind was responsible
for two heavy raids on our positions
northwest Of Thiaucourt on Friday
The boches attempted to gain the
same position in both attacks, but
were driven back each time with
heavy losses. Some OF the Germans
got through our artillery barrage.
but these were cut down by rife
fire or were bayonetted.


There has been no other infantry
hghting here for the past few hours.
Even the artillery activity has les
sened as the opposing armies take
cover in their newly constructed
trenches and dugouts.


American patrols continue to in
spect the Hindenburg line every
night These patrols also prevent the
Germans from exploring the areas in
front OF their wires.


The rear areas have been prac-
tically cleaned up. Huge boxes OF
captured German clothing, guns,
ammunition and other supplies are
being hauled to the rear. Refugees
are returning to their homes in re-
captured villages, after four years
absence, attempting to find their
houses among the ruins which have
been left everywhere. The dough-
boys are assisting in this work of
rehabilitation.


The Americans are more than ace

Mercier sent his wife and two dauEh-

behind to take care of their home,
expecting the enemy would soon be
driven out. For four, years the Ger
mans made him quarter officers in his
home and slave for them.


During the advance, the report sud-
denly reached the German officers
that the Americans were entering the
town. All but a major fed He ran
upstairs to pack his things. When
he came down American bayonets
caught him at the door. Following
closely upon the heels of the dough-
boys came Mercier's wife and dauEh-
ter. 1t was a glad reunion. Mer-
cier's family now cannot do enough
for the Americans.

LONDON, June 6.--Three passengers
and eight members of the crew are
missing from the steamer Kenilworth
Castle, which was severely damaged by
explosions after a collision. The steam
er, which carried about 30u passengers,
reached a British port Wednesday. The
passengers included Henry Burton,
South African Minister OF Railways
and Harbors, and other prominent
persons, who, however, were saved.


The collision occurred shortly after
midnight and was followed Immediate
ly by two explosions. The liner, which
previously had been damaged forward,
began to sink by the head as the fore
compartments filled with water. The
bulkheads, however, effectively kept
the vessel on an even keel, though
her bows were torn and twisted by
the force of the explosions.

Berlin, via London-German troops
have entered Odessa. This official
announcement was made Wednesday
night.


Odessa is the greatest Russian port
on the Black sea and the center OF
great agricultural section, the prod
ucts of which are desired to feed the
hungry peoples of the central en-
pires. The German advance through
Moldavia and Bessarabia has been vir-
tually unopposed.


Odessa is the fourth city of Russia
in population, was founded by Cathe-
rine ii in 1894. Its population num-
bers about 100000. nearly one-third OF
whom are Jews. Normally there were
several thousand German residents.
Among many other important institu-
tions it contains the Imperial New
Russian university, founded in 1865.


With Odessa safely in their hands,
the Teutons will have access to vast
stores of wheat which can be trans
ported overland or by sea to points
where it can be readily shipped into
Austria and Germany.


But the capture of Odessa will mean
something more-an advance over the
route to Persia and Afganistan and
possibly India, which is to be followed
now that the British have severed the
famous Berlin and Bagdad route to
the east.


Odessa's situation near the great
waterways of the Dnieper and the
Dniester makes it the natural outlet
70! the exports of the southwestern
provinces.


Despite the German peace, forced
upon Russia, and the announcement of
the Austrian premier in the Reichsrath
that Austria would take no part in the
German invasion into Muscovy, both
German and Austrian columns have
continued military operations, not only
toward Petrograd, but also toward
Odessa. Kiev was taken from the Boil
sheviki, and the Teutonic drive con-
tinued south.

warm blooded enthusiasm for the
soldiers of her strongest ally.

With the British Army in France,
April 26.-The great double German
drive in the Somme and Armentieres
sectors, which began Wednesday morn
ing, has developed into a terrifi~
struggle. The tide of battle has surged
to and fro during the last two days,
with the decision still in the balance.


The British, having been forced
back out of Villers-Bretenneux,
launched a counter attack and swept
the Germans back almost to the lines
which were held before the present
fighting began, and took over COO pris-
oners, and German dead are heaped
about the town.


The French have been driven back
out of HanGard-en-Santerre, but are
holding their positions close by, while
on the line southwest of Ypres, the
British have been compelled to with
draw slightly before furious attacks
along the Meteren- n-Bailleul-Wytschae
line.


Wounded Americans are arriving at
hospital behind the French line in
the Somme sector, showing that Gen.
Pershing's men are bearing their
share of the burden of the great battle.


Notwithstanding the frantic prepara-
tions made by the Germans for a con-
tinuance OF their drive toward Amiens
and the extreme violence of the fight
ing, their gains thus far in that region
have been very small.


Along the line from Albert south to
Castel, except at Hangarden-S Santerre
the German assaults have been hurled
back by the allied forces, which are
strongly posted on the higher ground
to which they retired during the last
days of the German drive in Picardy


1t is unofficially reported that four
to six German divisions, or from $4,000
to $4,000 men have been hurled at the
British and French lines near Ypres


The retirement of the British in this
sector must have been small, for there
are no great gains reported by Berlin
so far. 1t was rumored Thursday
that Mont KENNEL, a dominating
height north of Wulverghem, had
been taken by the enemy but this has
not been confirmed


That only slight gains have been
made anywhere along the two fronts
which have been subjected to attack
is proof that the allies are prepared
to defend their positions.


In the last three weeks the Germans
have hurried up heavy cannon to the
Somme battle ground and have
marched many fresh divisions to the
points where they have been held for
the moment of attack.


Raiding operations are reported
along the French lines east of Mont
didier.


Washington.-The number of Ameri-
cans killed in the German attack OF
April 20 near Seicheprey was less
than dozen and the number of in
jured was about twenty These fig
ures appeared to give support to the
German claim that 1873 Americans
were captured, since it previously had
been admitted that the American cas-
ualties were around 200

the hills and thus intercept the Italians
along the sPiave, whose sole line of re-
treat was these roads. The successful
strategy of Caporetto was invoked again.
Had it prevailed the Italians along the
Piave would have suddenly found them
selves threatened with development, as
did their comrades on the Bainsizza pla-
teau last year, after the collapse at Capo-
retto.


At the same time there was tremen-
dous push west at the point where the
Piave emerges from the hills and enters
the plain. Here the Italian, line makes
an almost complete right angle and
thenceforth follows the west bank of the
river southwark to the sea. At this
point there is on the west bank con-
siderable isolated plateau, from which,
were it in enemy hands, Austrian guns
could rake the rear, both of the Italian
troops on Monte Grappa between the
Piave and the Brenta and behind the
Piave from Nervesa southwark.


Montello heights, to give this plateau
it's familiar name, is the key alike to
the crossings of the Piave for many
miles southwark, to the highways sup
plying the front of the Piave and
to a vital portion of the front on che
hills. The push at Montello was the
main Austrian effort and not until the
Austrians had been driven from this high
ground toward the end of the battle was
the Italian victory assured. Most but
not quite all of Montello was ]at one
time in Austrian hands, portion was
held until the closing hours Of the often
sive, and at this point the Austrians
came within an ace of scoring a decisive
triumph.
headline:
Main Austrian Effort


Against Montello Heights

text:
No reports suggest that the Austrians
did not put up stiff fight or that the
Italians had an immediate and easy tri-
umpE The first days of fighting were
exceedingly severe and the Austrians
seem to have shown unusual contempt
for losses and unexpected tenacity. They
were beaten only because Italian morale
was even higher, Italian High Command
fully prepared and Italian numbers
equal to all demands. There was no
submerging of any sector, such as has
become familiar in German attacks in
France. Italian reserves were ready to
intervene before the forwards haG been
abolished. The familiar trench war con-
ditions seem to have prevailed, and there
was nothing approximating a break.
through, even at Montello, where the
Austrians were most successful.


Much was said of the work of British
contingents and something Of the service
of French units. But it may be doubted
if more than one British division was
present, and there was no great French
force involved. The Battle Of the Piave
was in the main an Italian triumph and
to the Italians belong the great credit.
In less than year Italy had remade her
army, and with the army the civilians
behind the line had been reorpanized.
All things considered, the blow was far
heavier than that which produced the
Caporetto disaster. Seventy-one divisions
were used, and these divisions were the
pick of the Austrian army, which had
been reconstructed for this effort.

LONDON, Nov. 11.-Waving flags
and cheering, an enormous crowd
pressed into Downing Street before
noon to-day, shouting "Lloyd George!
Lloyd George!" Finally the cheers and
chouts brought the Premier and An
drew Bonar Law, Chancellor OF the
Exchequer, to a second floor window
of the Premier's residence. When they
appeared pandemonum ensued.


For five minutes the crowd cheered
and waved flags frantically and then
they sang, "For He's a Jolly Good
Fellow" The Premier stood passive
and unsmiling, but his face was Sc
rene. When order and silence had
been obtained he said:


"You are entitled to rejoice. The
people of this country and Of their
allies and the people of our overseas
dominions and of India have won a
glorious victory. 1t was the sons and
daughters of the people who have won
it. 1t is the most wonderful victory
for liberty in the history of the world.
Let us thank God for it,"


Bonar Law Declines


Premier Lloyd George bowed and
disappeared. Chancellor Bonar Law,
after kissing his hand to the crowd
IS he pulled down the window, moved
! away.


Hardly had the Premier finished
talking when long file Of shouting
soldiers-British, Canadian, Austral-
ian, American and few from other
Allied countries-speared their way
through the throng and managed to
reach the front Of the Premier's house,
whore they gave him a great ovation.
Colonel Winston Spencer Churchill,
Minister of Munitions, was given an
enthusiastic ovation when he ap-
preached the ministry in an auto
mobile. The crowd stopped the car
and climbed over it and Colonel
Churchill was compelled to make a
brief speech.


Firecrackers Alarm City


The firing Of the maroons (fire-
crackers which initiate the crack of
a cannon) by the firemen and police
startled many residents Of London,
whose first thought was that an enemy
air raid was in progress. They soon
discovered however, that the maroons
were signalling the signing OF the
armistice.


Some factories and munitions works
gave their employees a holiday imme-
diately the good news became known.


Bands and the pipers of the Scots
Guards paraded through Whitehall,
playing martial and patriotic airs.
They were accompanied by singing
crowds, who time and again sang the
national anthem.


The official centre of the British
Empire was the scene of many demon
strations Seldom before have the
streets of London been paraded by
such hilarious swarm of people as
to-day.


King Makes a Speech
a great multitude waving flags ap-
peared before Buckingham Palace
shortly before noon and cheered until
the King and Queen, Princess Mary
and the Duke Of Connaught appeared
on the balcony. King George said:


"With you rejoice. Thank God for
thc victories which the Allied armies

The Austrians yesterday failed
again to make more than minor
gains in their great drive against
the Italian line, although they are
attacking with more than a mill
ion men.


Throwing fresh reserves against the
Piave River front, on the Italian
right, the enemy made his only
advances. On the critical noun
tain front he abandoned his at
tacks and fell back at several
points before fierce Allied counter
blows.


Thirty thousand prisoners are
claimed by the Austrian War
Office. But observers on all fronts
point to the tremendous loses in
flicted on the enemy's forces and
to the small Allied casualties. All
reports indicate the exaggeration
OF the Austrian report prepared
for home consumption.
Along the Piave the fighting con-
tinues with greatest intensity.
Unable to bring his artillery across
the river in the heavy fighting, the
Austrian infantry has stormed
forward short distances against
smaller forces of Italians. Ter
rifle Austrian blows west of the
Piave in front of Maserada were
sanguinarily repulsed by the Ital-
ian defenders. Enormous losses
were inflicted on the enemy.
South of Montello hill, on the mid
die Piave, the Austrians advanced
less than a mile, pushing toward
Maserada. On the lower Piave
the enemy pushed forward about
two miles beyond Capo Sile, fore
ing the Italians back to the Fos-
setta Canal, about fifteen miles
from Venice.


On the Montello, in the centre Of
the battle line, the Italians forced
the enemy back toward the river
and strengthened their line against
new assaults. Further west.
among the mountains, the Allied
armies broke repeated Austrian
assaults, and in counter blows
gained ground on the east side of
the Asiago Plateau.


More than $500 prisoners were
taken by the Allied armies in the
fighting.

The Hudson is disgorging its ice, and
the sea gulls are taking free excursion
trips down the river


The spring movement. which began
Wednesday night, continued in an UNI
tidy and desultory fashion throughout
yesterday. Rats and powders Of ice,
fiat and expansive, barely showing
above the surface of the water, or jut-
ting like buoys out of the stream,
foundcred in tho tide Of the lower
North River all day long, not a men:
ace, but a nuisance to navigators,
Every now and then fcrryboat would
have to make dctour around 40
loot or 100-foot cake, which might
have bruised a propeller or spraincd a
shaft.


Barges and lighters, going upstream
under the power and guidance of har-
Dor tugs, had to pursue a snakelike
course to avoid the ice New York
Harbor tugs are icc-shy these days.
Tney have been boxing with old Borcas
all winter long, dividing their time be-
tween frozen ferry slips and hospital
wards in the drydocks.


They Are Now Veterans


There was az time-not more than
five or six weeks ago-when these same
tugs had to force gangway through
Staten Island Sound and Kill Van Kull,
jammed with ice that had foated down
from the temperate regions of The
Bronx and Yonkers, and propeller
blades snapped like match wood and
stout engine shafts were tied into
knots. The ice now drifting seaward
comes from the polar regions of
Poughkeepse and Albany, and it's
tough.


Thus far no damage has been done
beyond that wrought in the first at
tack Wednesday night, when the under
plnnlng of the Recreation Pier and the
Manhattan Line pier. at 129th and
l3Uth Streets, was ripped out, and the
cadets aboard the naval training ship
Newport were joStled out of their
hunks. But everything along the North
River is in danger. New foes arc break

and they are all headed for New York
City.

Dock Commissioner Murray Hubert
yesterday laid his plans for the reccp-
tion of the ice foes. He consulted
with Colonel S. W. Roessler, United
States army engineer in charge of Dis
trict No. | Of the llarbor Line Board,
and il was decided to send feet OF
the old iceramming tugs. which did
such valiant service during the winter.
TO meet the foe.


When big jams up the river get
under way Commiss oner Hubert will
be notified by telephone, and the tugs
will be dispatched to break up the ice
and herd the big cakes in midstream.
The government tug Manistee will lead
the attack, accompanied by railroad
tugs Commissioner Hubert plans to
tow some of the huge cakes down
stream, if such a plan is possible


Every cake and chunk that drifted
downstream yesterday was mounted by
flock Of sea gulls. screeching loudly.


The ice danger, it is said, will last
about week

ON THE FRENCH FRONT IN
FRANCE, July 1.-THE superbly ex-
ecuted local action carried out by the
French to-day southeast of Amiens not
only gave them a large batch of prs-
oners, but brought into their posses
SIGN the entire Rouvrelles Plateau.
dominating the region between the
rivers Avre and Moreuil and the MOVE,
through which the main railroad from
Paris to Aniens passes, and which has
been in the hands of the enemy since
March.


More than 500 German officers and
men already captured have been sent
to the rear, and others are arriving.


The artillery preparation preceding
the attack was brief, but it was of a
powerful character and the aim of the
gunners was so accurate that when the
infantry went over they found the
trees in the small woods Astounding in
this vicinity reduced to matchwood


The Germans had laid widespread
network of barbed wire in these woods
and the shells had blown the wire
into great tangle, making the prog
ress of the attackers most difficult. The
French troops, however, overcame the
almost impossible obstacles by gall
liant perseverance while under the in
cessant fire of hundreds of machine
guns.


The assault began early in the morn
ing and lasted three hours. The
Frenchmen advanced at some places to
a depth of 1900 yards along a front
extending for nearly five miles. The
village of Castel first fell before the
dashing attack, Anchin Farm next sue
cumbed and Groshetre Wood and
brouettes Wood followed Then Billot
Wood was captured. All these posi-
tions were taken despite the most de-
termlned opposition of the enemy, who
seemed firmly decided to hold the no.
sltlons at all costs.


The feat of the French troops was
all the more remarkable as, between
the two extreme points of the opera-
tion-Senecat Wood and Arriercour
Wood-the ground is broken by hills
and deep ravines where the enemy had
good shelter and was able to concen-
trate his forces without being seen.


Nothing, however, daunted the French
infantrymen, and they carried the DO
sltlons with courage and dash which
took them considerably beyond the oh
jectives set for them


The Germans suffered heavily in
dead and wounded, in addition to pris-
oners, while material and machine
guns were captured in considerable
quantities. The advance has given the
French good observation posts from
which they can see every movement
of the enemy along the main roads
and in Moreuil and Mailly-Raineval
region which was the scene of the
severest fighting in March and April.

FRANCE, Sept. 1.-The American
troops in their drive beyond Juvigny
last night and to-day advanced about
two miles and captured nearly 600 pris-
oners, together with considerable war
supplies.


Again the German defences north Of
scissors have been cracked by the
Americans, who tonight have made Sc
cure their new positions near Terry
Sorny and on line along the Bethun-
court-Soissons road.


The Americans are still at the apex
of the Allied forces in that part of the
general front, and the commanding Off
GER, the French General Mangin, to-day
supplemented his messages of con-
graduation, expressing to the American
commander admiration for his units
work and frankly admitting slight sur
prise that troops comparatively new
should have conducted themselves with
such dash and brilliancy.


The advance from J,gigny began at
4 o'clock Saturday, and the Americans
had gained their objective by o'clock
at night. Ragged points in the new
line were smoothed out to-day.


In addition to the 600 prisoners two
pieces of artillery were captured and a
great number Of machine guns and
trench mortars. Trenches, she'll holes
and the open field were strewn with
German dead


Field Day for Americans


The drive forward from the positions
north and south of Juvigny proved a
field day for the Americans and their
allies, the French. The artillery
blasted a way through the enemy ranks,
tearing down defences and levelling the
ground, while Allied planes maintained
complete and uninterrupted connection
by radio with battery commanders
throughout the engagement.


The infantry, when called upon for
it's part in the dramatic venture, re-
sponded like veteran troops after a
long period of rest, and with enthu-
slastic shouts began the pursuit OF
the Germaqs who were not caught in
the terrific barrage.


With the infantry went the tanks
and it was a different story from
that when they first advanced against
Juvigny. Two companies, thirty
tanks, had been detailed for the work
They were light, twoman French
tanks, capable of speed over rough
ground of ten or fifteen miles an
hour, and almost as easily handled as
an automobile. Their work was per-
formed admirably and full advantage

New York City climbed aboard the
artoist's equivalent of the "water

there with fair success throughout the
first "gasless Sunday" that ever dawned
On these shores since the original Adam
of all motorcraft fooled his way UP
Fifth Avenue.


Fuel Administrator Garfeld's official
request that gasolene be saved as one
more war measure apparently hit the
public conscience of the metropolis.
From the outlying regions of the city
came reports that the great motor high
ways, which on Sundays TEEN with
automobiles of all descriptions were
virtually deserted.


Where hundreds of thousands of
automobiles and motorcycles are ordi-
narily III use on Sundays, burning up
fuel now needed for airplanes and tanks
and other war craft, there were only
scores yesterday. And these scores of
motorcars carried the most unpopular
and most unhappy pleasure seekers
that were ever seen abroad in New
York City. In few cases demonstra-
tions against automobile parties verged
on riots.


Violators Jeered


All automobile parties that looked
like pleasure parties were greeted by
catcalls and boots far and wide. Even
soldiers in autos were not immune to
sarcasm from newsboys and other
youngsters, who made it their business
to enforce Fuel Administrator Gar
fields request. In few instances old
and useless eggs and tomatoes accom-
panied the remarks of Americas
youth. The motorists lot was not a
happy one.


Fifth Avenue displayed perhaps the
greatest number of taxicabs and auto
mobiles. They passed along this polite
thoroughfare with comparative i'm
munity, but not without unfriendly
starcs from persons along the sidewalk


Long Island motor highways were
practically deserted. Along these roads
only scattered few cars were seen.
while on former Sundays motors glided
back and forth by the thousand from
early morning till long after midnight.


1t was an ideal day for motoring. A
cloudless sky and cool early autumn
breeze conspired to tempt the man who
owned anything on wheels to take to
the road. But it required brave man
to venture forth in a gasolcne-driyen
vehicle.


The police hardly lifted a finger to
prod the conscience of the selfish.
They did not have to do so. That part
of the days programme was attended
to by several thousand young men in
knee breeches, bare feet and endowed
with maximum lung power and mini
mum modesty.


"Slacker!" "Hun lover!" "Kaiser-
ite!" were some of the yells which
greeted the few automobile parties
that ventured out. The newsboys.
whose patriotism lies close to the sur
face and extends all the way to the
marrow, forgot all about their papers
when they saw what appeared like a
"joy-riding" group. Down at the Bat
terry and other ferry points where
automobiles sought egress to the coun-
try the newsies enjoyed the best oppor-
tunities for batting the gasolene slack
ers.


Near Riot at Battery


At the Battery one of these demon
strations led up to dramatic climax
which threatened to end in a riot.

ing at "a Washington Street, advanced

DOVER, February 15.-The weather
was thick and the night was very dark
when the German destroyers dashed
upon British patrol vessels in the
Strait of Dover early Friday morning
and sank eight of them. The patrol
vessel. being equipped only with light
armament for anti-subnarine work, did
not have a chance once the Germans
got among them.


The risk thus taken is shared by
great numbers Of trawlers and drifters,
operating in all weather and at all
hours. Yet the proportion Of losses has
been remarkably small.


On the latest occasion the crews bore
themselves with the same coolness and
courage that drifter men have shown in
innumerable circumstances OF danger
and difficulty. In one noteworthy Incl
dent drifter was shelled at close
quarters by two German destroyers,
whose thirty-pound shells killed all of
the crew except two and set the drifter
afire. The two survivors, seeing their
craft ablaze and believing it would
sink. launched a boat. They had not
rowed far when they saw the vessel
was still afloat and the enemy retiring.
They returned, put out the fire and
brought the drifter to port.

forces, General Won Falkenhayn quit
his command and returned to the Turk
ish capital in disgust. according to off
cial dispatches received here to-day.

units for several months, had under

ations. Of this number more than so
per cent deserted on the way, accord
ing to estimates of General Allenby.
Forty-one companies of storm troops
which left Alexandretta 300 strong
each reached the front only 100 strong
each, the British commander reports.

men in refusing 70 go on, recognizing
the decentralization in the ranks. When
the expedition was three days out of
Constantinople the German commander
gave up hope and returned.


The dispatches further state that
typhus is making enormous inroads
into the Turkish army, nearly 80 per
cent of the troops being lost through
the disease

Eight months in stormy Russia has
been the experiences OF Miss Bessie
Beatty, as a representative Of . san
Francisco newspaper. The newspaper
woman spoke at the Woman's party
headquarters last night.


Russian women a. . whole diner
little from their American sisters,
she said. They are content to be the
BACKGROUND against which their men
folk play the exciting parts in life.
Confent to Pour Tea.


They are content to sit behind the
sanovar at the meetings OF the po-
Htical parties and pour tea They
enjoy wearing red bands on their
sleeves and ushering the members 70
their seats. They revel in doing the
necessary clerical work and all the
drudgery, in spite OF the fact that
since the inception of the revolution
they have been granted equal rights
and privileges with men.


There are a few women" she con-
tinued, who stand out from the mass
but they are the unusual types.


She mentioned four. and sketched
their romantic and often tragic his
tories. They are:, Nine. Breshko-
vasye, grandmother Of the revolu-
ton: Nine Botchkarova. leader OF
the Battalion Of Death: Marie spiri-
donova. the girl who shot the tyran-
nical governor. was exiled to Siberia
and who afterwards became leader OF
the Russian reyolutionists.


She poetieaily described the atti-
tude Of the Russian people towards
their revolution.


TrampIed Their Liberty.


The Russian people first looked
upon their revolution as a beautiful
butterfly. They dared not touch it
at first and watched in wonderment
its actions. After a while they be-
gan to brush the sheen from its
wings and finally trampled the beau-
tiful butterfly of freedom under
rough-shod feet"


Miss Beatty, representing the San
Franciscan Bulletin, was present at
the Winter Palace when the provis-
ional government was arrested at .
o'clock in the morning. She was
the only woman permitted aboard the
Russian feet since the revolution.
and one of the few women allowed
to visit the front lines Of the Rus
sian army.

Italian air experts for his excellent

one of a bombing squadron that was
intercepted before it reached its OBJ

When Lieutenant Fitch observed
enemy planes rising to the attack he
dropped his bombs on two of their
aviation camps and then started back
for the Italian lines. While still about
thirteen miles inside the enemy terri
tory the five Austrian scout planes
overlook him from the rear He was
without support, as the other bomb
ers in his formation had preceded him
toward the home hangar.


Lieutenant Fitch, who was acting as
pilot, dived in order to obtain the max
imum speed, and then pursued a zig
gag course in the race for the Italian
lines. Meanwhile, his machine gunner
maintained bursts of fire at the pur-
suers.


One enemy plane came down in a
dashing attempt to destroy the bomb
ing plane and passed within twenty
five feet The enemy's fire was mac
curate, but that of the lieutenant's ma
chine gunner was true, and the scout
plane went into a swirling nose dive
to the earth.


The four other Austrian airmen at
tackled in turn from varying distances.
but the fire from the bombing plane
each time frustrated their attempts.
Finally Lieutenant Fitch's escort saw
his predicament and returned, driving
away the Austrian scouts.

from which a Bolshevik pompom had

The Americans debarked at dawn from

lagos UP stream.


After trudging five miles over p road
deeper in mud than those in Flanders.
through struggling villages. runner
directed the contingent to slip through
wooded swamp TO the flank Of the
enemy.


The guides led the water soaked, mud
coated soldiers single file mile after
mile through the Tundra. which one
American described as a big. soft pud-
ding. The soldiers jumped from one
moss hummock to another, across clear,
cold puddles. but plunged in up to their
thighs where the hummocks were in
frequent


The soldiers were picking blueberries
as they advanced silently. They heard
the Bolsheviki talking and laughing
Behind the trees they formed a sklrmish
line within a hundred feet OF the enemy


Suddenly they were discovered The
Bolsheviki shouted, Shoot them! They
are behind u.s." There were scattering
SHOTS and then came a Gathering all
along the line, the Americans shooting
hard and fast as they lay fiat hugging
the ground they had CURSED on the march
but which was now protecting them
from the bullets whistling overhead.

LONDON. Aug. 21.-A British and a
German submarine met recently. The
enemy had crossed the North Sea, pen
etrated British waters and was wait
ing to pounce upon any ship that might
cross its track. The British boat was
returning to its base after hard
cruise.


Both boats were on the surface, but
the British boat picked up the enemy
and dived before she herself was
sighted. She fired two torpedoes, and
through her periscope an explosion was
observed. Coming to the surface five
minutes later, the British crew found
one German swimming in the wreckage.
tie was the captain of the enemy. The
other officers and the crew had gone
down in their boat.

River directly north of the CITY of

Piave protect the important City of
Treviso, which is only fifteen miles
north of Venice.

that another Austrian attempt yes
terday to take the important Tonale
Pass was prevented by the Italian
batteries.

discarded by the men for the first time

camps were decorated with rolls of
bedding being given an airing. Men
and horses basked in the sunshine in
the streets and on the hllsides -
grateful experience after the winter
damp chill.

hung out to dry, tent flaps and hut win
dows open and hospital patients
breathing the sweet spring air. Mean

paved and lighted. There is a con-
stant stream of traffic, and the Sleep
lest old women who haunt the streets

through the streets.

ment have been organized. The old
fashioned oil lamps in the streets
have been replaced by electric lights.
The water supply has been improved
and extended. Mosques have been re-
paired. roads have been paved, and
schools, including a training school

in dry weather and sanitary officials
have penetrated the most hidden cor
ners Of the city. The municipal gov
ernment has been made self-support-
ing.


across the Tigris river. These are

with British occupation and come

Anticipating the warfare of tanks
the Germans soon developed ways
and means of dealing with these
moving forts. In the front line
trenches they installed their So
called antitank guns wherever the
ground out front was favorable for
tank maneuvres. 1t appears that
they employed discarded artillery for
their anti-tank defences; cannon
which were worn out through con-
slant firing and which were there
fore no longer accurate for long dis
lance work, but were still available
for firing point blank at advancing
tanks. So the Germans must have
cleaned their military household, and
the collection of ordnance odds and
ends was dispatched to the front.


That helped some. Numbers of
Allied tanks were put out Of action
in various attacks. And with typi-
cal Teuton self-pride they did not
fail to announce the fact to the world
Forthwith the Germans placed the
tank in the same category as the
extinct dodo.


Then came General Byng's sur
prise attack in front of Cambria.
Heretofore tanks had been employed
to accompany infantry waves during
an assault, helping them to get
across bad ground and to attack ma
chine gun posts and centres of re-
sistance. The usual artillery bonn
bardment Of several days or even
weeks had always been employed
until that time on the Western front
since the advent of trench warfare.


But General Byng dispensed with
artillery preparation. His prepare
tons and concentrations were car
ried out with the greatest secrecy
On front Of over twenty-five miles
he sent his fleets of tanks into battle,
followed by dashing British infan-
try. The tanks went through he
stout German belts of barbed wire
and the infantry followed. Caught
completely by surprise, the German
troops were simply rushed off their
feet before they could get their anti
tank guns into action and call for
the support of their artillery in the
rear.
