LONDON, Aug 6.-The attempted raid

Anglian coast last night was a complete
fasco according to reports thus far re-
ceived.


British fliers were ready for the Wis
itors and met them well out at sea,
bringing down one in flames. damaging
second and driving a third away.
What happened to the other two airships
III the squadron Is not disclosed in the
off1cial statement. The fact. however,
that the report said, "Zeppelins crossed
the coast is ground for the presumption
that these did reach land.


There Is no evidence as yet that they
dropped any bombs. and 1t is probable
that their crews were kept busy protect
ing their ships against pursuing British
airmen.


The novel feature OF the raid was the
early arrival of the airshps. Two OF
. them actually were seen approaching the
coast by holiday makers from the prom
enade of widely known seaside resort.
1T is considered possible that the Ger
mans miscalculated their visibility and
by arriving before dark invited an easy
defeat.


Airplanes Immediately went into pur-
suit. and the Zeppelins, throwing out
smoke clouds, turned northward and en-
deavored to escape. They were over
taken about forty miles from the shore,
and just before midnight one was
brought down In flames and another
damaged.

The triumphant march to the Rhine
by the armies of the allies has been
going on steadily all week. At last
these brave troops move forward real
ly with bands playing and banners
flying" and as they pass through the
cities, towns and hamlets of northern
France and Belgium the people of
those places. released from years of
barbarous slavery to the Huns, give
them hySterical welcome. From holes
where they had been hidden since the
summer of 1914 their national flags
are brought forth to decorate the
buildings and streets and the ruins
left by the invaders, and everywhere
homemade specimens of the Stars and
Stripes fly with the other banners.
The wild joy of the inhabitants is
pathetic in the extreme, and especial
ly In Alsace and Lorraine, which Is
occupied by the Third American army
together with the French under Cen
eral Mangin. Those lost Provinces
now regained have ever remained
loyal ut heart to France and they wei
coined the Poilus and the doughboys
with open arms.


For Lorraine the great demonstra-
ton took place In Metz, which was
entered by Mangins army on Tuesday.
That general was injured the day be-
fore when his horse fell, but Marshal
Petain was there and, standing before
the statue of Marshal Ney in the main
square, reviewed the troops. The In
habitants hud overturned the German
statues in the city and made the place
gay with the allied flags and with
their own national costumes. Similar
scenes were witnessed In Strassburg
and other cities of Alsace. Near the
Swiss border the French troops first
reached the Rhine.


The American army of occupation,
commanded by General Dickman, and
about 250000 strong, marched across
the old German frontier into Lor-
raine and swung to the nortEward
into Luxcmburg, the marines on its
right passing into Belgium. In the
grand duchy no less than elsewhere
the Yankees were enthusiastically
greeted. Their advance was made al
ways with due caution, however, and
the task of moving so large an army
forward steadily and keeping up its
supplies and communications was
performed in perfect manner.


Meanwhile the British and Belgian
armies of occupation We're keeping
pace with their allies, advancing
through Belgium close on the heels of
the retiring Germans.


-tA-


Everywhere the victors found vast
stores of weapons and materials
which the Huns left in accordance
with the stipulations of the armistice,
and in general it was said the Ger
mans were carrying out the terms i'm
posed on them. There. was pillaglng
in some places, and occasionally a
storehouse was blown up, but these
instances were comparatively infre-
quent. The worst charge against the
conquered foe related to the released
allied prisoners. Many of these.
usually sick and half starved were
merely turned loose to make their way
to their friends as best they might.
England sent to Berlin stern pro
test against such violations of the ar
miStice terms.


The allied fleets have passed through
the Dardanelles to the Black sea, and
a1ied troops have been landed in Con-
stantinopIe aud on the Galllpoli penin-

AN ATLANTIC PORT, April 80
veritable "hell ship" the barkentine
John G. Meyer, with two of her crew
dead of scurvy, and the rest suffering
from the disease, has reached this port,
with Captain Henry Kruger the only
person aboard left to navigate the ves-
sci. A third member of the crew died
soon after the ship came into port,
while six others are critically i'll in
the Marine Hospital here.


The disastrous trip of the Meyer
started three months ago from Skonda,
British West Africa. In February the
scurvy began to make it's appearance,
and among the first OF it's victims was
sixty-eight years old, whose home was
with his sister, Mrs. Sophie Lehr, at
9 Hamilton Avenue, Brooklyn.


For month the mate fought off the
disease, then succumbed on March II,
and was buried at sea. The rest of the
crew were down with the disease by
this time, and Captain Kruger's log
records the fact that the men were too
weak to send the shrouded body over
the side, ana had to make many at
tempts before it was put over the rail.


Then, with the entire crew crippled,
the barkentine ran into a storm On
March 81. Not a hand was moved to
make the vessel ready to ride out the
gale. The seas climbed over her sides,
the wind ripped off sails, rigging and
masts. Practically a wreck, the John
C. Meyers wallowed for three days in
the trough of the sea, with Captain
Kruger at the wheel, doing his best to
keep her nose straight.


One Of the sick sailors, August Laine,
rose from his bunk after the storm had
passed, and helped Captain Kruger rig
up jury mast, by the aid of which, in
five weeks, the barkentne reached this
port. Laine, worn% out by his heroic
effort, died a few days later, the sec
ond victim of the trip.


The cook was among those taken i'll,
and all the food eaten had to be cooked
by the mon themselves. Lack of nour-
ishment aggravated the ravages of the
scurvy. When the ship reached this
port, flying the two yellow flags calling
for the health officers, all Of the crew
were taken off. Charles Anderson died
a few hours after removal to the hos
pital

Does ice convey infectious diseases? This is of
high importance in the summertime when prac-
tcaly every household ice to keep foods fresh
and when it comes in contact with many of our
foods before them.


While heat will kill such water-borne germs as
those of typhoid and cholera it has been found
that they resist cold for long time.


Scientists have frozen large numbers of typhoid
germs in water under laboratory conditions and
have found many Of the germs alive after several
weeks.


In addition to such experiments sanitariums
have found that feces from typhoid patients when
thrown the ground during the and ice
periods of winter. remained dangerous until spring.


Ice made from pure water in factories which
kept clean and in sanitary condition and ice
which has been cut from reasonably deep ponds
lakes streams after natural freezing conditions
and stored under sanitary conditions are about
equally safe.


Ice made from polluted water, in dirty in
sanitary factories and ice that is from shallow
polluted ponds from grossly polluted rivers will
contain intestinal organisms and disease germs and
not safe, experts say.


Be on the safe side and do not let ice come in
contact with your food water.

Navy Department announced to-

Taking No Chances.

! the schooner Ef<vard R. Baird, jr.,

having escaped southwark through
the patrol fleets.


The fact that the submarines are
Drawing the dangers from the patrols
which are converging around the
area of operation leads officials to
believe that the raiders are waiting
ior much bigger prey than they have
yet found. The place where they
nave operated most recently is in the
lane of travel up and down the coast
End through it must pass much of
TIE important shipping going in and
out Of the Virginia Capes.


The sinking of the Harpathian
brings the total of vessels known to
have been sent down on this side of
the Atlantic by the raiders to
iourteen-six steamers and eight
sehooners. All the vessels were
american except the Eidsvold ard

If you were little girl. just at the

Consuela Garcia, an attractive sixteen

Consuela. with her sister Elesia, who

All through the day and night while
they tossed about the ocean in the lit

Carolina with thirty others of the pas
sengers and crew Consuela never took
her arm from around Elesia's shoulder
And as the rescuing boat made fast to
its pier and the passengers started down

bered what she had been told.


As Elesia started on a run down the
tricky swaying gangplank. Consuela
called to her:


Now Elesia, be careful or you'll fall
You know you're always stumbling"


But moment later when Consuela
herself spied her mother and her
brother, Michael. a black-haired little
lad. she forgot all about her caution and
fairly few into the outstretched arms
waiting for her. But there wasn't any
one to be found who could scold her
even a little bit. They were all too busy
telling how brave she had been.


Only Consuela wasn't giving thought
to what she had done or said She was
too much concerned with those two
trunks way out there somewhere on the
bottom OF the Atlantic Ocean.

coast. with unknown results, accord

the captain of Brazilian steamship.

South American port, sighted the sub
marine soon after 10 o'clock. Inn
mediately full speed ahead was order
ed, and the vessel zigzagged. A few
minutes later a vessel in the distance.
which later was identified as United
States Army transport, open fire on
the submarine. Two shots were heard,
followed almost Immediately by three
others.


The submarine was too far away.
said the South American captain, for
him to tell whether any of the shots
took effect He also said that he
thought the transport was too far
from the submarine for the latter to
try hit with torpedo.


The Brazilian steamer continued its
courst with all possible speed for
this port without waiting to ascer-
tain the result of the encounter.

Americans. The Germans tonight are
in retreat beyond the Freya positions.


The Germans have retired so rapidly
at some points that the Americans have
experienced difficulty in maintaining
contact with the enemy.


More than sixty cannon, scores of
IT'S, dozens of 1908, numerous howit-
zers of various calibres and hundreds
Of machine guns were captured by the
Americans during the advance of Fri
day and Saturday. Vast quantities of
ammunition and war material of all
kinds Fell into their hands.


General Pcrshing's forces west Of
the Mouse this afternoon captured
Fosse. This represents an advance of
four miles from the starting line
through Bayonville.


The Germans gave little if any indi-
cation Of an impending retreat until
this afternoon. All morning long the
Americans on every part of the front
had met with stubborn resistance.


The opposition was especially de-
termined on the left and right, and the
American centre had pushed forward
considerably further than had either
wing. Though the centre had intended
to continue and to attain its days OBJ
jectives, it was apparent there soon
would have to be a pause if the troops
were not to be fanked.


Good News Doubted


SO certain were the military COM
manders that the Germans would not
break that the chief Of staff of the
troops in the centre belittled the re-
port arriving about 2 o'clock this after
noon that the town Of Fosse had been
taken.


One hour later, however, reports be-
gan to come thick and fast. The first
showed that resistance against the
American left had unaccountably
ceased. Then came reports indicating
that the right wing was moving ahead
at marvellous speed.


This morning, despite the increased
volume Of the enemy fire, the Ameri-
cans were steadily advancing, although
more slowly than on Friday. The line
at noon showed no losses of territory,
while some improvement of it had been
effected


Resistance Grows Weak


The first intimation that the enemy
was retreating came from the Fourth
French Army, which was advancing to
the northeast. Within a short time va
rious American units from all parts Of
the line announced that they also were
advancing and were finding the resist
ance, which was so marked all morn
ing, melting away on the right. Even
troops in motor trucks had not been
able to catch up with the enemy.


The Americans were not slow in fol-
lowing the advantage on the left wing,
which had met with the most serious
resistance, and began to press forward
imme diately in the Bots des Loges on
the heels Of the Germans, cleaning up
all who Jagged behind They pushed
their line northward for nearly mile.
Champigneville, strong point in the
Freya defence line, had been taken
earlier in the day, and the troops who
had rushed it pressed forward and
swept through Verpel, after partly sur
rounding the town.


In Rain and Mud


Through rain and mud the Americans
advanced toward Thenorgues, a mile
and half north of Verpel. The enemy
had been expected to hold there, fol-
it was strong position, but very little
resistance was met with when the vii.
lage was entered.


Troops further to the right continued
their victorious march and fought thei,
way beyond Buzancy to Fosse, a strone
poitn nearly seven miles beyong yes
terday's starting point and two and s
half miles north Of Bayonville.


Bayonville is an important strategic
point, known as the heart of the Frevs
Stellung. With it's capture the Ameri
can troops had broken the Germans
| last organized defences.

market, but to send them gradually
and thus prevent flooding the market
which will result in heavy spoilage.

w the phantom airmen fly,
A ghostly squadron of the clouds that sweep
the Flanders sky.
They haunt the fields of Picardy; they
know the Marne's red flood
The crimson poppies Of the plains are dyed
with their hearts blood
Like grim gray shades, their soundlcss
planes in battles angle lined.
Above their comrades trenches cross: and
ere they leave behind
The friends they love, they dip down low
then swiftly upward shoot
To pass the staff that held the Aag-a silent
proud salute.
Then on they fly beyond the lines that hold
the hated Huns;
Immune from searchlights' deadly stare and
eagle-hungry guns;
And each one fights his fights again, the
conflicts that he won,
Until the last, when from the sky his shat
tered pinons spun.
They are the men who died for France
who from the heavens blue
Crashed thunderbots that even Jove's red
anger never knew
They killed their foe, in turn were killed.
and died with smiling breath
Brave youths, who drained the cup Of Life
to pledge a toast to Death.
And every Allied fighting man who sees
their ghostly planes
Feels some new strength and courage surg
ing, thrilling through his veins;
But every German heart is chilled; the
phantom fliers drear
Plunge in his heart blade Of steel-a
vague and nameless fear
These noble souls, these vagrant spirits.
nevermore can rest,
But nightly through the fatal skies must
ever wing their quest;
They, may not know the endless peace NJ
Deaths sweet dreamless trance
Until the Hun is driven from the sacred
soil of France.

THE efficiency and economy of


Marshal Foch's strategy are


strikingly illustrated in the
enforced retirement of the Germans
from the Lys Valley salient. Cen
eral Won Arnims armies are draw
ing out of this pocket of their own
motion. The German situation fur
Their south compels them to retreat.
They are giving up, under merely
nominal enemy pressure, territory
whose capture cost them a mighty
effort and entailed severe and fruit
less losses.


The German offensive in Flanders
last April attained unexpected sue
cess in its first stages. The shock
Of the initial attack fell on a Portu-
guese division holding the line about
Armentieres. These troops broke
and a gap was made through which
Won Arnim's forces pushed far up
the fiat Lys Valley. They were not
held for many days. The German
advance continued due west for
about twelve miles, to the edge of
the Forest of Nieppe. Then Luden-
dorff turned his attention to bullying
out the sides of the salient.


He had little luck on the south
side, where the British First Army,
under Horne, held like a rock at
Givenchy and on the line west COW
ering Bethune. But on the north the
Germans took Messines Ridge, Wyt-
schaete, Neuve Eglise, Bailleul and
Mont KENNEL and seemed to be on
the point Of capturing Ypres and
compelling a British evacuation of
the whole of the old Ypres salient
About two-thirds of it was, in fact,
evacuated.


The Germans threatened the road
to Dunkirk and Calais. Field Mar
shall Haig issued an order telling the
British troops that they were fight
ing with their "bacls to the wall"
and General Maurice made his
famous query Che has since ex-
planned that it's import was entirely
misunderstood in America), "Where
is Bliicher?" The situation was not
saved until French reserves arrived
at KENNEL and Dranoutre and Gen.
eral Won Arnim suffered his bloody
reverse southwest of Ypres on
April 20.


The Germans have held the Lys
Valley salient for four months and
half. But they have not been able
to turn it's possession to any advan-
tage. Now they are sinking out of
it-sullenly, without any choice on

LONDON, Sept lit has been
learned that the Germans now have
only 1856 divisions on the Western bat
tlefront, as compared with 204 which
they had recently. They had to break
up eight divisions to form drafts. They
are endeavorng to make up this short
age with two or more Austrian di-
visions and large amount of Austrian
artillery.


The enemy has put into the present
battle, north and south, about ninety
one divisions, of which seventeen have
been engaged twice. The Germans
also have made several changes in the
High Command, at least two command
ers having been removed.


The German Grown Prince is said to
have been deprived of half his army
corps, the men having been transferred
to General Won Boehn.

erly direction as far as the Aisne

The hoodoo that has clung to Joseph

make flight to boost the Liberty

tune to tragedy yesterday.


Two thousand school children gath

way to watch the air fighter soar aloft
and wing away toward Manhattan, saw
the machine catch fire. and then, when
the blaze had been extinguished. saw
it's whirling propeller whip the life
out of Max Bessiler, the mechanic.


Stehlin was scheduled to fly at 1O:30,
but the plane. Berckmann Scout, was
not ready for the flight. It's inventor,
Maurice Berckmann, and Bessiler
worked for more than an hour, tuning
it up.


Shortly before noon, the first acci-
dent occurred. Bessiler was spinning
the propeller, when in some manner
the gasoline that had been spilled on
the ground, ignited. In an instant the
machine was a mass Of flames. Men
fought the fire with blankets and coats,
and finally beat it out after the ma
chine had been scorched, but other
wise not injured.


Berckmann then mounted to the
pilots seat, and Bessiler began to twirl
the propeller again. Stehlin stood a
few feet away, dressed for fight, and
awaiting the smooth running Of the
engine before taking the inventors
place.


Presently the engine roared into life
Bessiler stood directly in front of
the whirling propeller, listening to the
drone that scaled higher and higher
as the speed of the motor increased

signalling Berckmann to open the
throttle to the limit. The inventor
obeyed, but the powerful drag of the
propeller was too great for the blocks
holding the machine. 1t surged for
ward over them. The blades revolving
with terrific force caught Bessiler
lifted him from the ground and flung
him ten yards away.


The mechanics right arm was
severed from his shoulder, his left was
broken and he sustained other in.
juries. He died in a short time.

Miss Helen Rice, the girls junior

capturing the open tourney at the West
Side Tennis Club at Forest Hills. Long
Island, yesterday. The Chaplin School

tournament play was Of great aid in

steadiness throughout the match and
romped about the court to intercept

shots. Many long volleys featured the

Hooker would end The fight by driving
into the net. number of the other
games brought out spirited playing, also
gong to deuce several times, before
Miss Hooker would find it difficult to
get Miss Rice's drives over the net.

and returns to the back baselnes that

hooker could not return the ball prop
erly. In the second set, Miss Hooker

The Germans were thus, after June A,
in possession Of the roads leading to
Paris, both east and west of the Oise
West Of the Oise they held the line Mont
didier-Noyon, east of the river they held
the front Soissons- Chateau Thierry, but
the two wings were still separated by
the French centre, which retained pos
session of the high ground in the angle
between the Disc and the Aisne. Not
until the Germans west of the river had
pushed south to the crossings of the Disc
and occupied Compiegne could the whole
front be joined and become active


For the moment no advanceowas pos
sible on the Soissons- Chateau Thierry
front, because the French had brought up
reserves and possessed admirable interior
communications, while the Germans had
moved into country whose communica-
tions had been destroyed and had outrun
their reserves and supplies. Thus, while
it was possible that the German might
first indulge in some side show, compar-
able with his Flanders venture after his
March push in Picardy, it was reasona-
bly, plain that when he resumed his drive
for Paris he would attack upon the west
bank of the Disc and on the front be-
tween Montdidier and Noyon, and this
is exactly what he did last Sunday. By
this time he had had two months to re-
pair his communications west of the
Disc and collect the munitions and sup
plies for new attack.

Old King Sol was striving with all

to force his radiant face through the
clouded sky and cast the shadow which
will send poor old Prof. Arctomys
Monax, the grounding, back into his
hut for forty more days of inclement
weather.


The professor came forth from his
obscure hole Somewhere in Washing
tom early this morning. and. pushing
the snow from his door. peered first at
the sky and then at the ground A
heavy cloud hung over the city and
there was every indication that old
Sol was sleeping late


With an encouraging farewell to Mrs
Monax and the little ground hogs, the
old professor hurried to the weather
bureau to inquire if anything had been
learned from the astronomic instru-
ments as to what Sol was planning for
the day.


The forecaster, who has learned from
experience that Soils mind is as change
able as the winds, told the anxious pro
fessor that the smiling old man appa-
rently had his back turned to Wash
ington. but might shift his position at
any moment.


The ground hog returned to his hole
riveted his eyes on the sky and sat
waiting for the hour this evening when


Sol must disappear behind the horizon
| In the west.

with the volume of credit constantly
increasing

WITH THE FRENCH ARMIES, July
26.-How the German higher command
intervened suddenly on July 21, hold
ing between five and six hundred thou
sand troops in the SossonsMarne
Rheims salient, instead of evacuating
this highly dangerous g>pund precipi-
lately under Allied pressure, was
learned by The Tribune correspondent
to-day.


The decision was taken while the
troops were in full retreat from the
southern end of the salient, and it
changed the entire character of the
battle.


The Germans crossed the Marne on
July Is OH a wide front, and penetrat-
ed southwark short distance against
Franco American resistance. The
troops carried three days rations, ex-
pecting revictualment and reinforce
ment from the north bank Immediately.


Cut OFF From Supplies


Instead, the constant bombing of
their bridges by the Allies cannon fire
placed them in a serious predcament,
without supplies of all kinds, after
three days of fighting.


On the morning of the 18th the big
Allied counter offensive was launched
from the Aisne to the Marne, imperl-
ling the safety of those on the south
bank. A retreat was ordered and car
ried out Friday.


Sunday morning at 3 o'clock the
masses of heavy German guns on the
ncrth bank which had been pounding
the Allied lines on the south bank sud
denly ceased firing. Airplane observa-
tion at daybreak showed the enemy
troops and guns flowing along north
ward in general retreat.


Allied troops advancing from the
west, north of Chateau Thierry, forged
, ahead rapidly, their progress being op-
posed only by the enemy's rear guards.
Chateau Thierry, outhanked on the
north, fell. The Allied advance along
the entire line was deep. Some ele-
ments of both French and American
troops bridged the Marine and crossed
from the south bank.


Enemy Line Stiffened


Then early Monday morning as sud
denly as the retreat began the Ger
man resistance stiffened. The heavy
guns were hurriedly replaced in posi-
tion and began firing. The Allied
bridges over the Marne were DESTROYED.
Enemy counter attacks at many points
on the line indicated the complete
switch in the German plans.


Since Monday the Allied advance, as
Tribune readers are aware, has made
smaller daily progress against severe
resistance. Fresh enemy divisions
have appeared, though the Allied guns
are able to hurl shells from three
sides into the salient, blasting provi-
sion centres, troop formations and
conveys alike. at the same time harass-
ing almost the entire area OF the
salient constantly from the air.


Enemy troops, fighting under such
conditions since Monday, slowly giving
way before the Allied advance. have
suffered terribly, mostly in dead and
wounded. Some of the prisoners still
being taken are identified as belonging
to units which retreated from the
south bank of the Marne almost a
week ago. They. unanimously admit
suffering horribly. Their morale is at
a low ebb.

tieth Street and Broadway when they

localities. When they first came to

followed later by Daly's, at Twenty
ninth Street and Broadway; the old
Princess, and the old Bijou, in the
vicinity of Thirtieth Street. Then
they moved further uptown and turned
Thirty ninth Street into the theatrical
centre by taking the Casino Theatre
and building on Thirty~ninth Street the
Thirty-ninth Street Theatre, the Max
inc Elliott Theatre and the Princess
Theatre. Next they took the Broadway
and built the Comedy and the Lyric
theatres, thereby invading the neigh
borhood Of Forty-second Street.

By thu Associated Press.


ITALIAN HEADQUARTERS IN
NORTHERN ITALY, Thursday. January
Italian troops have succeeded in
breaking the pressure which the enemy
has been exerting on the lower Piave
In the sector nearest Venice. This Is q
triangular sector originally cleared of
the enemy when the whole region was
inundated by opening the canals. But
recently low water has permitted the
enemy to renew his incursions almost
to Capo Sile and the Venetian lagoons.


Enemy patrols had established dug
outs and posts in tn elagoons at Agen-
zia Zuliana, just across the river from
Capo Sile. which commands the canal
running to Porto Grande and the re-
gion back Of Venice. During the early
days of the week the italian navy had
bombarded the dugouts and destroyed
the bridge on which the enemy was
attempting to cross at Agenzia Trezza.
The enemy made repeated attempts to
enlarge his position, but was uniformly
repulsed.


Brings Full Force to Bear.


Stung by the repeated checks the
enemy brought his full force to bear
yesterday morning. They were met by
chosen Italian troops from the Gren-
adler and Bersaglieri brigades. The
Italian defense was led by the Bersag-
lieri, who had asked that privilege in
order to answer seurrilous pamphlets
which had been thrown into the Italian
lines.


The Bersaglieri hewed their way to
the enemys support lines. The fight
was stubborn for the first two hours,
but the enemy gradually gave ground
as fresh ranks of Bersaglieri, cheering
and singing patriotic songs. threw
emy was finally pushed back from the
positions he had gained.


Ruse Used by Enemy.


One of the favorite ruses used by
the enemy was for party of his troops
to advance with their hands up. calling,
''kamerad!" When they would get
close to the Italian lines they would
rush forward suddenly with hand
grenades. but to be moved down as
they advanced by the Italian machine
at close quarters.


Heavy losses were sustained by the
enemy and the Italians captured $50
prisoners. The battle-ground was COW
cred with Austrian dead. and burial
parties were busy throughout the
night burying the bodies.


Many individual instances of brav-
cry stand out. In one case an Italian
officer and five men leaped into an
Austrian trench, took two machine
and brought back the guns.


The Italian success gives a serious
check to the enemy effort to improve
his position near Venice.

urday when a pitched battle was

Soviet forces surrounded the build

ference. The populace derives solace

The accident happened when the two
trains ran past each other at Saybrook.


The locomotive responsible for the
mishap was hauling srain No. 105, and
was just leaving the station when the
express came by on the next track. The
valve was forced out under heavy
pressure, and the escaping steam ex-
ploded with roar and swept through
the windows of the three rcarward
Pullmans.


Passengers suddenly aroused by the
scalding blast left their berths in q
panic, and several are said to have
been kept from jumping from the
broken windows by the prompt action
of trainmen.


The express was stopped and ran
back to the station. and doctors were
summoned from the town and neigh
boring villages along the line. Two Of
the injured were taken to the Saybrook
Hospital. The others, after emergency
treatment, were carried on to New
London.


The two passengers treated at the
hospital were Miss Molly Murphy, Nor
wich, Conn, and Alden M. Farris, a
porter, Cambridge, Mass. Both were
badly scalded and suffered cuts from
broken glass.


Railroad officials here had no ex-
planation for the accident. The head
Of the broken valve weighed about a
pound, and was driven through two
windows of one of the sleepers, passing
out on the opposite side of the track.

Paris, July 31.-American troops
fighting north of the Ourcq river on
the scissors. Rheims salient have en-
larged their brilliant victory of Mon
day at Sergy, where they cut 10 pieces
divisions of Germany's picked troops
and took and held the village against
counter attacks.


Notwithstanding continued heavy
opposition by guns, machine guns and
large numbers of the enemy, soldiers
from the middle western and eastern
states drove their line northward
from Sergy Tuesday for a distance of
about two miles and were resting at
night oil the slopes approaching the
woods beyond the town of Nesles.
Where they stood at the last accounts
the Americans formed the apex of the
long line running across the salient.


While the bitter fighting was in
progress between the Americans and
Germans, the French on both SIDES OF
the fighting front also moved forward
for goodly gains northeast of Fere-en-
Tardenois and east of Sergy.
In the Nesles forest the Germans
are holding strong positions from
which they are shelling, but thus far
ineffectively. the menacing allied line
before them.


| Prussian guards and Bavarians were
in the thick OF the fighting through
out Tuesday, but again they were out
Unanswered and outfought by the
Americans and again suffered heavy
casualties.


The Germans apparently are on the
eve of attempting to end their retreat
from the Scissors Rheims salient and
turning and offering frontal battle in
force to the entente allied armies.


The day of rear guard actions seems
drawing to close Violent counter
offensive measures against their an
tagonists already are in progress by
the Germans over most of the battle
| front.


Further gains have been made by
the allies only after the bitterest fight
ing Standing firmly and giving
ground only under absolute necessity,
the allied troops everywhere have ex-
acted huge toll.


In the center of the pocket, north
fof the Ourcq river, the Germans in a
counter attack drove the Americans
out of Cierges, but this slight gain was
more than overcome later by the pene-
tration of the Americans northward
from Sergy Beugneux, lying on the
west side of the pocket northwest of
-Tardenois also was taken by
the Germans, but later the French and
Americans recaptured it, and, with
Grand Rosy in their possession, they
still hold vantage points for a small
turning movement toward Fere.


Southwest of Rheims the Germans
delivered a violent attack against the
French from both sides of st. Euph-
raise. Their effort to capture the vii
lage, however, was futile, altho they
pushed their line slightly forward on
the west side of 1t.


| The Rome report says: ION the
whole of the front there has been re-
ciprocal artillery fighting. In the Giudi-
caria and Val Arsa hostile parties We're
repulsed Along the Piaye our recon-
noitering patrols brought back enemy
arms and material. Thirteen hostile
aircraft have been brought down.

Ludendorff's chief fight in France has
been against time. He is striving to get
decisive results before the new American
armies arrive in force


He is winning territory But,he is not
making any progress in his race against
our troop ships. Since March 21, when
the first great German offensive, that
based on St. Quentin was launched, the
United States has sent 100000 men to
Europe. That half million practically
offsets the losses of the Allies in the last
four drives.


General March announced yesterday
that the American troops now abroad
number more than 100000. This total
includes non-combatant services and COM
batants in all stages of training. But
by the happy device of brigading the
newer units with French and British
commands, training has been greatly ac-
CELEBRATED. General Foch is apparently
greatly pleased with the showing made
by our units on the Picardy, Marine and
Lorraine fronts. Hence his decision to
withdraw the units now fighting with the
French and British and to create indie
pendent American divisions and armies.


We have now two completely organized
divisions-one under General Bundy and
one under General Bullard. Two of our
divisions of 10000 men are enough for
an army corps. Two corps-120.000 men
are enough for an army The German
division has, on an average, less than
$4,000 men, the French division less than
$4,000 and the British division less than
$4,000. Even if our present somewhat
topheavy organization is retained, we
can soon have two complete American
armies ready TO take over distinct sectors
Of the front.


Our troops at Cantigny and northwest
of Chateau Thierry have shown the finest
fighting quality They ought to show it.
for they are picked men, with plenty Of
initiative and high morale They are
more than match--man for man-for
the Germans, for much third and fourth
rate material has been swept into the
German ranks since 1917.


BY July we ought to have 100000
troops in France-more than 100000 of
them combatants. Our men are now only
getting their baptism of fire AS fully
organized American divisions, corps and
armies they will soon be in the thick of
the coming German offensive. The Ger
man High Command knows this The
German soldiers and the German peoplc
don't know it. The Kaiser has been
promising the German public victory ODE
fore the Americans arrive" That prom
Use has been blasted We are already
arriving. Unless Ludendorff can reach
one of his main detectives before the end
of July, his hot race against time and
our transatlantic transport service will
be lost.

validcd groups will be repatriated.

Thrilling incidents marked the flight
of a small party of Americans from
Petrograd through the battle lines in
Finland on their way to Stockholm. ac-
cording to report just received at the
State Department.


They suffered all sorts of privations
insults and dangers.


A twenty-two-year-ol girl. Miss

the Stars and Stripes and a flag OF
truce to persuade the white guards to
stop firing.


The refugees left Petrograd at a time

Germans were approaching closer and
closer and hostile airplanes were rain
ing death from the skies.

The Americans who proceeded to
TammerfoFS eventually received spe-
cial train from the Helsingfors author
tiles. but as the train was about to pull
out soldiers took possession, all bag
gage was dumped out and the Ameri-
cans were arrested. They were later
allowed to proceed under guard of red
troops and eventually Joined forces
with other Americans at Bjorneburg
from where they went to Mentyloto
close to the battle lines.


From Mentyloto Capt. Crosley. Mr.
Tyer and Miss Ranta started in a
sleigh for the front. Capt. Crosley
mounted the breastworks with the
stars and Stripes, Mr.. Tyer took a flag
of truce and Miss RantI acted as in
terpreter. When the firing ceased they
walked between the lines and were met
by volley. the white guards believing
their advance was ruse. None was
hit. but Miss Ranta was taken pris-
oner. being a Finn.

during which sleighs from the red
guards took the Americans and their
goods and dumped them midway be-
tween the lines where the white
guards picked them up.

Miss Ranta, meanwhile, had discov-
cred In the commander-in-chie of the
whites an old schoolmate, of who she
demanded that he allow the burial OF
many dead whom the refugees had OBJ
served between the lines. The reds
claimed that the whites had fired OIL
Red Cross workers who attempted to
rescue the wounded, who had died. Her
request was granted and she herself
was ordered released.


The refugees proceeded overland in
sleighs, through bitter cold, and met
with many insults from German officers
and Finnish soldiers under their in
fiuence.

NEW YORK. August THE torrid
weather in which New York is swelter-
ing caused two more deaths and nine
additional -prostrations during the
twenty-four hours ending at II am
today. At that hour the mercury had
touched 81 degrees and was expected
to climb still higher, which would
break all heat records for the year.


The weather bureau forecast thun-
dershowers soon, with temporary re-
lief, but announced that in all prob
ability the metropolis was certain to
suffer one more day Of high tempera-
ture


New York Stock Exchange members
circulated petition, which was being
signed generally. asking the board Of
governors to close the exchange from
Friday night until Monday owing to


The usually congested districts Of
New York were almost deserted to-
day, thousands Of mothers and chill
dren flocking to the beaches. The
police estimated that thousands Of
persons slept last night on the sand
at Coney Island and innumerable
others found refuge in the city's parks.

PHILADELPHIA, August There
was no relief here today from the in
tense heat. At noon the thermometer
touched 100 degrees, six higher than
at the same hour yesterday. The
maximum yesterday was 1922. -Four
deaths. and numerous prostrations
were reported.


The high temperature is having its
effect upon Industrial plants, the Hog
Island shipyard and other establish
ments, hundreds of workers being
forced to quit.

Maps at the weather bureau this
morning showed that the heat wave
now extends across the country from
New York to Chicago. with Pennsyl-
vania and Maryland carrying the. se-
verest part


The one redeeming feature of the
situation in Washington. it was said
at the weather bureau. is the fact that
the humidity has been slowly going
down in the last twenty-four hours,
indicating that the moisture in the air
which makes the temperature so op-
pressive, Is being absorbed.

crowded last night with the thousands
of strangers in the city, who could
not stand the oppression in boarding
house rooms


Ice cream parlors and drug stores
cream manufacturers had difficulty in
keeping their customers supplied

State. War and Navy departments,
with its thick stone walls, did not
escape the heat Of yesterday and to-
day, owing to its crowded condition
and the fact that even the corridors
are filled with clerks and typewriters.


Yesterday about nifty clerks in the
building succumbed to the heat and
were given medical attention in the
emergency room in the basement.
About the same number were taken
three today for treatment. Nearly all
the patients were women. Capt. will
liams Of the Army Medical Corps, who Is
in charge OF the emergency rooms,
said that none of the cases was seri-

able to be taken to their homes after

door suffered the most.

With the advent OF the automobile,
the city limits lost much OF their pop
uiarity, writes Desire Lescauhoura, IN
The Hotel Gazette The speedy ma
chint, in carrying It's occupants way
out into the country before they could
feel the pinch of thirst or hungar, has
diverted that kind of trade into new
country. Wide-awakc bonifaces who
guessed right and opened well-con
Quoted roadhouses within radius Of
ten to forty miles from the city are
well rewarded now for their foresight.


Last month | took a stroll through
Central Park and was sadly impressed
by the loneliness of our magnificent
playground. The weather was very
cold, the drives covertd with snow, and
not a soul was to be seen walking or
conspicuous by his invisibility. What
a contrast with the Central Park of
a quarter of q century ago! What good
sleighing could be had; you could then
see continuous string of sleighs gld-
ing merrily over the drives, enlivening
the park with the sound of their bells
and the joyous voices OF the riders.


The two park restaurants, the Casino
and McGowan's Pass Tavern. were then
fairly crowded. At the tavern (Which
was torn down last year the long since
departed Gabe Case, its landlord, was
on deck ever, sleighing day, sitting in
the hall close to his celebrated par
rot, greeting almost every newcomer
by his first name. He seemed to know
everybody. The cafe especially was
we'll patronized on those days. Quite
a number of the old Hoboken Turtle
Club members used to meet there.
stories, like that of the old mare with
the false tail. and the quail-eating con-
test, were rehashed for the twentieth
time or more. and drew as much APP
plause as if related for the first time.


With their appetitcs sharpened by
the keen, frosty air, and a few drinks,
the jolly fellows would also feel like
having something to eat. Most of them
were satisfied with the bountiful free
lunch which was frequently passed
around Others (shocked at some Of
the noisiest ones, who, after ingurgi-
tating six cups OF clam broth. half
q pound of cold corned beef, liberal
slice of sage cheese sandwiched be-
tweentwo large chowder crackers, had
always their minds occupied some
where else when came their turn to
treat), would order dinner, rightly
thinking that the landlord should also
make some money out of his restaI-
rant.


This was quite naturally the SOUP
selected being also one of the Tavern
specialties. Two heipings of that soup
were enough to satisfy ones hunger.
Such delicious soup can hardly be
found anywhere nowadays. Not be-
cause our cooks cannot make it. but be-
cause our present clear green turtle
soup, with its transparent amber color,
looks by far more attractive and. con-
sequently, is much more popular, es-
'.secially with the ladies'.


The old Hoboken Turtle Club soup
certainly did not look appetizing in
appearance to the uninitiated, being
turbid and of dark greenish color,

WITH THE AMERICAN ARMY IN FRANCE,
Oct. s.-The American First Army has
now been fighting In the wooded and
picturesque Montfaucon and Argonne
salients northwest Of verdun nearly two
weeks. We have recovered upward Of
thirty small towns from the Germans.
encompassed and taken about a dozen
small woods, have penetrated into the
Argonne forest and have captured pris-
oners. guns and ammunition in SUFFICIENT
number to proclaim the success Of the
operation as far as It has gone.


In the fighting on front. approximate
ly twenty-five miles long. we have made
an average gain Of Ave miles, in some
places ten. and all this, has been done
In inclement weather. Not a day since
the enterprise started on the morning
of September Is has been without rain
somewhere along our lines. Some days
1t came down in torrents for twenty-four
hours, creating almost impossible roads
and drenchlng our brave soldiers to the
skin. Yet they have enever faltered.
Soldiers From Many states.
Troops from Pennsylvania have pre-
dominated in the undertaking. there
being more soldiers from the Keystone
State thar any other. Between the Meuse
River and the Argonne forest men from
different States lined UP in mixed Or
der, including some from Virginia and
Maryland and some from Pennsylvania;
then divisions from all the States; then
more Pennsylvanians. and then troops
from Illinois, Ohio. Washington. Oregon,
Missouri and Kansas. with New York
men at the extreme left.


That was the lineup at the start. The
average time for attacking troops to
stay in the front line II Ave days. Since
the fighting began other units were
sent In for relief at different places along
the line. including troops from prac-
tically all the States. Many negro regi-
! ments participated and behaved splen-
didly.


The reader must try to picture the
troops from all the States spread out In
a great crescent, pushing forward
through woods and villages, up hill and
| down, crawling through barbed wire
entanglements and always faced by ex-
| asperating nests OF enemy machine guns.
The greatest difhculty encountered by

| would press beyond. thus keeping our
artillery officers constantly worried for
| fear they were not dropping the barrage
| far enough ahead. The French officers

| the Americans to exceed orders with q
never failing establishment


It was this eagerness to press ahead
that caused seven companies to be cut

ON THE FRENCH FRONT IN
FRANCE, July 12.-The superbly ex-
ecuted local action carried out by the
French to-day southeast of Amiens not
only gave them a large batch of prs-
oners, but brought into their posses
SIGN the entire Rouvrelles Plateau.
dominating the region between the
rivers Avre and Moreuil and the Noye,
through which the main railroad from
Paris to Aniens passes, and which has
been in the hands of the enemy since
March.


More than 500 German officers and
men already captured have been sent
to the rear, and others are arriving.


The artillery preparation preceding
the attack was brief, but it was of a
powerful character and the aim of the
gunners was so accurate that when the
infantry went over they found the
trees in the small woods abounding in
this vicinity reduced to matchwood


The Germans had laid widespread
network of barbed wire in these woods
and the shells had blown the wire
into great tangle, making the prog
ress of the attackers most difficult. The
French troops, however, overcame the
almost impossible obstacles by gall
liant perseverance while under the in
cessant fire of hundreds of machine
guns.


The assault began early in the morn
ing and lasted three hours. The
Frenchmen advanced at some places to
a depth of 1900 yards along a front
extending for nearly five miles. The
village of Castel first fell before the
dashing attack, Anchin Farm next sue
cumbed and Groshetre Wood and
brouettes Wood followed Then Billot
Wood was captured. All these posi-
tions were taken despite the most de-
termlned opposition of the enemy, who
seemed firmly decided to hold the no.
sltlons at all costs.


The feat of the French troops was
all the more remarkable as, between
the two extreme points of the opera-
tion-Senecat Wood and Arriercour
Wood-the ground is broken by hills
and deep ravines where the enemy had
good shelter and was able to concen-
trate his forces without being seen.


Nothing, however, daunted the French
infantrymen, and they carried the DO
sltlons with courage and dash which
took them considerably beyond the oh
jectives set for them


The Germans suffered heavily in
dead and wounded, in addition to pris-
oners, while material and machine
guns were captured in considerable
quantities. The advance has given the
French good observation posts from
which they can see every movement
of the enemy along the main roads
and in Moreuil and Mailly-Raineval
region which was the scene of the
severest fighting in March and April.

text:
CONSIDERABLE smoke where there


was no fire appeared last week as


the result of a report that the
mails had been closed to the March issue
of "The Metropolitan Magazine" owing to
an article by William Hard entitled els
America Honest?" The postmaster at
New York got letter from Washington
which was intended to put him on his
guard and cause him to examine "The
Metropolitan" and similar magazines in
the future before dispatch. Owing TO
misunderstanding, the postmaster at New
York notified THE Metropolitan" that the
March issue was unavailable. Then it
transpred that the government had not
ordered any such ban, nor was the gov
ernment considering the revocation of
"The Metropolitan's" second class mail
ing privileges.


The mistake. however, revived interest
in the relationship Of the American press
to the war censorship and the matter of
criticism of the governments prosecution
Of the war.


1t will be recalled that early last sum-
\
tated over a proposed press gag law"
After more than month Of excitement,
mild bill was passed and the incident was
forgotten In the fall, however, the pres
ent espionage act, much more drastic than
the first bill, was passed. Yet SO recon-
ciled has the country become to the ne
cessity for secrecy regarding military af
20; fo,
lications that the passage of the second
bill hardly raised ripple on the stream of
journalistic comment.


Apparently, the reason was that, until
Congress late in 1917 began its investiga-
ton into the conduct Of the war, the press
CT the country had practically withheld
severe and partisan criticism of the gov
ernment. But the Congressional investi-
cation into the arms, munitions, shipping
and other situations restored the tongue
of the press, and the most severe criticism,
both partisan and nonpartisan, began to
appear.


Even more notable was the appearance,
along with the demand for a War Cabi-
net and Ministry of Munitions, of the
IL.
Previously the President had been prac-
tically immune, but since the agitation for
reorganization in the War Department his
critics have come out into the open. Only
when many friendly critics joined the nat
ural partisan critics Of the Administra-
ton was it apparent how very consider
able difference of opinion between the
country and the President had accumu-
lated in nine months.


When, therefore, it was reported last
week that the March issue of "The Met
ropolitan" had been unfavorably criticised
by the Postoffce Department, it appeared
that the matter Of restrictions on tho
American press passed definitely out of
the realm Of criticism designed to hinder
the prosecution Of the war-that is scdi-
tious critjcism~-and had entered the field
OF "patriotic" or "advisory" criticism. For
it was cited, "The Metropolitan" could not
possibly be classcd with various other
newspapers and magazines which had been
denied second class mail privileges for
printing of-color criticism Of the war
Ever since August ! 1914, this magazinc
has been rabidIy pro-Ally, and demanded
war with Germany following the sinking
OF the LuSitania. Uisplcagure With "Thc

Metropolitan" it was insisted, must
therefore have come from reasons other
than those usually termed patriotic if
outward appearances are to be trusted.


The difference between "The Metronoli-
tan" and numerous other publications that
have come under the ban is easily seen.
Many Socialist organs, such as "The
American Socialist" and Victor Berger's
paper, have had their second class privi-
leges withdrawn. Representing triAe
"wilder" views is Max Eastman's
Masses" now revived as "The Lberator."
Many German-language publications re-
ceived similar treatment. Moreover, when
Victor L. Berger and four others were in
dicted last week, they were charged with


obstructing recruiting by voicing their op-
position "cFiehy by misrepresentation
subtlety and indirection, revealing what
they would pretend to conceal and hiding
disloyalty to the United States behind a
screen of specious and evasive phrases"
In the past "The Metropolitan" has not
been ranked with this class of periodicals.

German airplanes, flying at a low

American trenches.

took the air, bringing down two of
the enemy planes and dispensing the
others. All the American airmen re-
turned safely.


No Americans were taken prison
er, but three Germans were capt
ured.


The correspondent viewed the bat
tie from hill short distance be-
hind the lines. Trains moved to the
front with great regularity and
scores Of huge shells were seen
bursting, throwing up clouds of
white smoke in the neighboring hills.

PARIS. August 10.-The effect Of
American rife nre has been one of
the great surprises to tho enemy dur
ing the recent engagements along the
front. AS a result the rife is fast
coming back to its own as the de-
pendable weapon for infantry fight
ing.


For time its place was challenged
by the hand grenade. Some English
and French experts took the view that
the grenade would gradually super
sede the rifle. Trench warfare had
accustomed both sides to the grenade,
SO that the rifle was seldom brought
into use.


Even with the two weapons availa BILE
the troops had become accustomed to
use the grenade rather than the rife.
An enemy fugitive would often be
chased until his pursuer was near
enough to throw a grenade, when .
rife ball would have brought down
the fugitive from q distance.
All this has been changed, however,
by the open fighting Of tho present
offensive and the unusually effective
use the Americans have made Of the
rife. Gen. Pershtng has maintained
from the first that the ride was the
indispensable weapon for infantry.
While the grenade has not been neg
lected, every American unit has been
thoroughly trained in rifle practice.
Many national guardsmen, as we'll as
reuglars were crack ride shots, win
ners in tournaments and veterans of
the rifle ranges maintained at home,
These ranges have become a notable
feature Of the training on this side,
until the whole American organiza-
tion has become specially proficient
with the rifle.


German prisoners all recount the
same story, that the greateSk surprise
came from the impetuosity of the
American troops, and after that that
the sweeping fire of the American rifle
caused the greatest CONSERVATION and
loss. Accustomed to waiting for a
grenade attack at close quarters, the
mass formations of the enemy were
suddenly exposed to concentrated rifle
from a trained marksman who was
not blazing into the air, but was pick
ing out his target and sending his
ball home


This experience has fully sustained
the American contention for the rifle
as. against the grenade. French and
English military experts are agreed
in the enthusiastic approval they give
the Americans as rihemen, ana in the
view that the rife has again dcinon-
strated its right to be considered the
paramount weapon for infantry fight
ing.

The thrilling story OF how the Boy
scouts of Cracow saved their city,
Polands most ancient and noblest
center, was made public here yester-
day by Polish agents who received
reports from the Polish-American sol
diers who have returned to Poland
from the Western battle front. Al
though the famous Boy Scouts brought
invaluable aid to the allies, particu-
ilarly in England, the records OF the
international organization bear no
brighter nor more courageous ex-
ample Of heroism than that of the
Polish boys who shouldered rifles and
guarded the ancient hearths of their
fathers.


When the Austrian empire fell, ac-
cording to the reports received here,
the Austrian officials and soldiers in
Cracow vanished at once. The city
was left without leadership. its or
ganization for the preservation of law
and order fell apart and its treasures
were left unguarded before the greedy
eyes Of any bandits or marauders who
might gather in its streets


1t was then that two scoutmasters,
trained army officers. whose loyalty to
the cause of Poland and whose hatred
for Germany led them to refuse serv-
ice in the Austrian army, rallied the
Boy Scouts of the city. The leaders
also impressed into service some old
men who were sworn in as police.
They had no uniforms and were iden-
titled as officers Of the law by cards
hung about their necks. AS the serv-
ice was compulsory these ancient po-
lieemen could not be depended upon
to fulfill their duties.


The boys guarded the public
buildings, military depots and other
points. including stores of high ex-
plcsiye, which were sufficient to
have wrecked the city had they
fallen into the hands of the Reds.


Only these boys and another
youthful semi-military organization
with a few stray officers stood be-
tween the city and its treasures, in
cluding the gold-encrusted tombs of
the Polish kings. and the criminal
elements. which focked to the city
from every quarter. But the boys
did their duty well. They had one
battle with evil-doers. and their
victory brought to the citizenry a
not-to-be-shaken sense OF security.


Now that the allies have permit
ted the shipment OF some $4,000
trained soldiers from the Western
front to Poland. all fears for the
safety of Cracow and it's famous
university, which recently voted
President Wilson a fellow, have
passed.

noce dive to the earth. :.

regulations. Reams of paper were con-

them. They were of the most varied

mum prices and threatening rigorous
punishment for war-profiteering; laws

tain farm products to animals: laws

card for everybody to make it posi-

up every possible opening through
which rebellious appetite might seek
its satisfaction.

necessary. The food shortage was
looming up and drawing nearer in such
threatening shape that nobody could
deny the urgent necessity for rigorous
rationing, for confscating supplies and
for carefully outstanding them against
waste or an unfair distribution.

night when she collided with the Brit

and landed here to-day

fog. The Livingstonia. outward bound

down the coast. With a great hole in

soon after the crew had taken to the
boats.

STOCKHOLM, May 1.-Reports that
KEN, the Russian seaport west of
Archangel on the Mourman railway
line, had been occupied by Finnish gov
ernment troops are denied by the
Finnish Legation here The legation
stated to The Associated Press corre-
spondent that the force which occupied
the town was from the Russian Karelian
home guard, this occupancy in nowise
threatening traffic on the railway.


Dispatches from Moscow in midApril
reported that Finnish government
troops had attacked the Mourman rail-
way near KEN, but had been repulsed
by the Entente forces which had been
landed at Mourmansk to protect the
railway.


Kullerwo Manner. an intellectual
leader of the Finnish Socialists and one
of the men responsible for the Finnish
revolution, was taken prisoner at
Vibcrg when the White Guards, or
Finnish government forces, recently
captured that Finnish port, seventy-five
miles northwest of Petrograd. The
correspondent who sent this informa-
ton says the Bolshevik Red Guards
lost 1000 men killed in the battle at
Viborg


Thornwell Haynes, American Consul
at Helsingfors, Finland, in report to
the American Legation here, gives a
more favorable picture Of conditions in
Finland. He recommends that America
send food for distribution in northern
Finland and expresses the belief such
a course might prevent the country in
clining further toward Germany.


The consul says that when the legal
government in Finland was overthrown,
Sweden refused help, other Scandi-
navian countries were unable to. give
aid and France, which alone of the
Entente Allies has recognized the Fin
nish Republic, could not get help there
in time. and nothing was left for the
Firms but to appeal to Germany.

New York, April 2.-German news
papers just received here record that
serious disorder attended the general
strike in Berlin during the last week
of January and the first few days Of
February.


For time the trolley car service was
interrupted in various parts of Berlin
because the strikers had repeatedly cut
the wires, Street car passengers were
attacked, women conductors were abused
strikers throwing stones at the women
and pulling them from the cars. Traffic
was blocked by strikers, who ran cars
into one another at full speed. Meat
stores were pilaged. bakers were forced
to supply bread without bread cards.


The strike came as a surprise TO the
leaders of the Social Democratic party,
said the Internatonaie Korrespondenz,
q Socialistic organ. which stated that
the party leadership had not been con-
suited regarding the strike. Later the
party leaders were requested by the
strikers to assume charge of the strike,
which they did in an endeavor to end
the strike as soon as possible and to see
to it that the interests of labor were
safeguarded


The strike temporarily paralyzed all
war industries i'm Berlin and vicinity,
especially the airplane plants. The Prus-
sian Diet was also affected as the COM
postors and printers there also Joined
the strike, thus interfering considerably
with the proceedings. owing to the delay
in the printing of bills and other docu-
ments.

Paris, Dec. 25.-"Please, Pere Noel.
let father come home!" has been the
Christmas prayer of every French
child for four years, and each year
they have been told the next Christ
mas the Jesus child would bring
Daddy" home. "Pere NOEL is the
French equivalent for Santa Claus.


Though the war is finished, peace
has not come. and for the fifth time
te French kiddies dream vainly OF
their fathers return, christmas failed
to bring the bearded Poilus home. The
war has lasted longer for France than
for America and most children
scarcely remember peace, when ZEN

goodies, and when mother didn't look
worried


Thus the first peace" Christmas is
similar to the war Christmas holidays
and even more so. The SOLDIERS are
still mobilized. The newspapers are
filled with rumors of new conflicts.


The peace terms as publicly dis
cussed are vaguer than ever.

WITH THE AMERICAN ARMY ON
THE NESLE, Aug. 6.--In the capture
of Fismes American troops took seven-
teen guns. These weapons and their
crews had been left south of the Vesle
to enflla1e an advance into Fismos
Some of the German artillerymen also
were captured


The Germans along the line onnosi+e
the Americans to the west. of Fismes
used their guns freely yesterday after
noon IN an apparent attempt to dis
courage the Americans and their
French allies from further aggressive
effort. The Germans we're handi
capped by the weather conditions. It
was misty, and at times rainy, and al
though the German balloons were up
they must have been unable to report
accurately on the Allied activity.
About mid afternoon the Germans
began trying other methods of get
ting the range for their heavy guns.
which they evidently hoped to use at
', night in interfering with the Allied
troop movements. Many shells which
threw out black smoke upon explod
ing were tired in the direction of the
crossroads and other objectives, the
enemy trying thus better to gauge the
range from the smoke clouds which
arose. The mist likewise worked to
hamper accuracy in observation on
these shells, which were of the time
variety, and after wasting numbers of
them the attempt was abandoned.


Gas Attacks Fail


Late IN the afternoon the Germans
began using mustard gas, sneeze gas
and some chocolate gas, the latter so
named from the odor given out nv tho
gaseous substance. These gas attacks
were ineffective. the American gas
drills having taught the troops all the
German tricks. Nevertheless. the Ger
mans were persistent IN this gassing
effort: They combed the hill border
ing the Vesle with their shells, en-
deavorlng to reach the roads leading
to Fismes and other points where thev
thought the Allies might be assem-
bling for a crossing of the Vese.


AT some places along the highways
the Germans would start planting gas
shells, and lay them down in zig
gag line for mile or so and back
again, often dropping the shells every
twenty or thirty feet, and then re-
peatlng the process along the road
way or other objective at which they
were aiming.


South Of Bazoches, one of the points
where the Germans tried this trick,
they fired lighter gas first, follow
ing it up with sneeze gas, and then
suddenly switching to more power
ful poison gas, hoping to catch the
Allies mapping. The men. however,
have learned TO discern the various
varieties of shells and their effects,
and have regular systems of sending
word along the line for each others
protection.


Gas Carried Back


To-day, likewise, there happened 10
be a south wind. which carried the
gas back across the Vesle, and. after
putting on their masks for each at
tack, the Americans would laugh as
the gas was blown back, and then con-
tinue about their business


Meanwhile the American and French
heavy guns to the south were sending
in repeated salvos, and the Germans
were supplementing their gas shelling
with their mine tnrowers and machine
guns north of the Vesle. These small
er weapons were kept working full
time, in the hope of keeping clear the
south banks Of the river. Darkness
came, and with it more rain. The
Germans kept pounding away after
dark, but for every she'll the enemy
sent in the Americans sent across a
half dozen or more, and never said
good night

lure OF a buttercup caused Mary Block,

votion with which she always looked
after her younger brothers. Philip, aged
5. and Charles, 4.

the buttercup blowing before a light
wind In a field beside the tracks OF the
West Shore Railroad. at Ravine road,
Jersey City. The other children were
Just ahead of her and apparently safe.
Mary turned aside, plucked the flower
and turned around.


In the moment her back was turned,
the tiny brothers had stepped over upon
the tracks. Beseng down upon them
was switch engine, running light. n
was SO close the engine driver had no
time in which to reverse the throttle.


Mary screamed but the babies paid
no heed. She ran upon the tracks and
gave the children a push that sent them
ST rawling TO one side. The engine struck
the little girl at the same moment, hurl-
ing her body twenty feet away. She was
dead when Frank Bowen. the engineer.
stepped down from his cab.


Although Mary's action undoubtedly
saved the elder brothers. life, the pilot
of the engine struck Charles a glaneing
blow and flung him heavily aside. He
was hurried to Jersey City Hospital.
where the physicians said he may not

Preliminary to the big drive the
guns beloved along a front of

the last barrier defending ancient
Ghent, with Brussels, the capital,
beyond.


German troops are shut off from
communication with the rest, but
they fought desperately and render

counter battery work was weak,
however. The Germans are known

Belgian advance.

poison gas which hung low because

barrage zone along the whole west

Belgians behind their artillery bar
rage. They crossed the canal twice
and were driven back twice by count
er-attacks. Then the Belgian artil-
lery was signaled to play a hose
stream of fire along the German
front line. Throughout the afternoon
the big guns launched an inferno of
death across the canal along a line
of forty miles.


The clouds were hanging low and
drizzling rain prevented the war
birds from observing. In the early
morning a flock of twelve German
machines made a short cruise over
the Belgian positions. Lacking fire
control. the German guns contented
themselves with sending shells and
gas over the known cross roads.

Swathmore, after tifteen-inning con-

to score, Houihan missing a difficult
fly from Carter.


Ogden, who twired for Swartmore
throughout, had control and speed
enough to last eleven innings and
struck out two of Columbia's Heaviest

seven hits, but retired ten in the long
game and gave only one base on balls.
koenig, the Columbia twirler, was
kept in the game for the entire eleven
innings by Coach Coaklcy and showed
no sign of slowing up until the very
end of the game. His good infield sup
port kept second run from being
scored in the last inning. He allowed
one more hit than his rival twirler,
but struck out only three men. Ogden
excelled him in nothing except greater
staying power.


Swarthmore started off the first inn
ing by scoring two runs, but the local
team tightened UP in the next and
held her scoreless for nine innings.
Columbia evened the score with a run
in the second and another in the sixth.
Goodman and Lester made the Colum-
bia runs.

fering internal injuries, which caused
her death in Bellevue Hospital The
right leg of Isidor Sohmer, elevator
operator, who leaped from his car to
save her, was torn off at the hip by the
descending car.


The dead woman lived at 1853 West
Fiftythird Street and had been visit
ing her sister, the hotel housekeeper,
on the twentieth floor. When she
reached the elevator shaft on her way
home the car was at the floor above
and the door into the shaft is said to
have been open.


After ringing the bell Mrs. Capthorn
lost her balance and pitched forward
into the shaft. Sohmer, who had
started his car down, saw her topple
and leaped in the hope of throwing her
back to safety. He missed her and
struck heavily on the threshold of the
shaft door.


The car descended upon his right
leg and amputated it. He retained con-
seriousness long enough to explain the
accident to the hotel physician. Both
the injured persons were taken to

East Fifty-seyenth Street

Some of US are much concerned about the "mor-
ale' of the boys who are going to the front, and
those who already there.
+ We are afraid they'll 60 to the devil because
they are being furnished with cigarettes, and
because they sometimes play baseball on Sunday.


But the fact is there is less venereal disease
among the boys in France than there is among the
boys at home.


They are far more interested in genuine religion
than they ever were in their native towns.


The job they're doing is burning out of their
lives the dross and the dirt that formerly elogged
their brains and their hearts,


They are giving themselves to \ task which
arouses the deepest, truest passion and patriotism


We need to be far more concerned about the
boys who remain at home than about the boys
who have given up everything to fight for demoe-
racy and freedom.


They have their own peculiar temptations, but,
other things being equal, they've got better
chance to come back whole-hearted and true than
the chap who remains at home for almost any
reason that sounds like = good excuse.


When the war is over, the sadest object in
the world will be the man who not only pitied
himself and allowed somebody else to do the fight
ing, but who assumed pietistie attitude toward
the soldier who passed through hell at the front
so that the Stacker might have comfortable time

w WASHINGTON, Aug. lS.-The food
situation in Germany VIII be bad this
winter. according to reliable advces
reaching Washington through neutral
countries During the summer the
food pressure has been relieved to Il
considerable extent by the availability
which the Germans must subsist dur
ing the winter are said to be III very
poor condition. in consequence the
people Of the Central Powers Will be
put to new tests of endurance this
winter.


German crops Will be successve!v
worse each year. agricultural experts
here declare. The German farmer has
practised intensive agriculture and has
in normal times secured. perhaps. the
largest yield per acre of any farmer
in the world. Intensive agriculture.
however. it is pointed out. requires
plenty OF fertilizer and much cultiva-
tion. Germany is now beginning to
feel q shortage Of both fertiiizing ma
ter!al and farm labor.


This spring German crops Were in
excellent condition during the early
growing season, but June was the cold
est month Germany has experienced 4
in many years. The thermometer went
down to 30 degrees repeatedly. and
there werS frosts which not only re-
tarded the crops but actually destroyed
much vegetation. July was very dry
for the most part, though toward it's
end there were heavy rains. These
conditions were far from ideal for good
crops.


From all the information available,
agricultural experts believe the German
grain crops are probably in very bad
condition. 1t will be impossible to fore
cast the condition Of the potato crop
until late this month. While it has
been popular belief that Germany
would obtain considerable food assist
ance from Russia. and from the
Ukraine in particular. officials here
declare that the Central Powers have
secured very little food from this
quarter. Germany hersel. counted on
finding valuable food surpusses in
Russia, it is stated but she found in
stead empty bins.


The explanation for this is to be
found in Two conditions which existed
IN Russia, prior 10 the complete break
down Of that nation. For months be-
fore Russia collapsed the Transports
ton systems feeding the armies had
been deteriorating. In consequence
the Russian army comnlssary had to
resort TO foraging, and therefore con-
sumed practically all food stocks in
the rich agricultural states close to
what was the eastern front.


The second factor which robbed the
Germans Of what food assistance they
might have obtained from Russia was
the revolutionary debauch in which
practically all the peasants indulged
after the fall of the monarchy. The
large landlords were disposscssed and
their holdings divided The peasant
farmers. instead of planting crops. pro-
ceedcd to celebrate their new freedom.
Russia produced little food during
1917 and the situation has been little
improved this year.


While the necessity for q military
decision on the Western front still will
remain. the food situation in the Cen
trail Powers may contribute good deal
to their eventual defeat. The feeling
OF the German people in this connec-
tion will not be improved by Herbert
Hoover's recent pronounccment that
the food crisis in the Allied countries
has been successfully passed.

spect the Hindenburg line every

the Germans from exploring the
areas in front OF their wires.

OF captured German clothing. guns

work OF rehabilitation.

ace-high with the Inhabitants.

boches invaded Thiaucourt in 1914.

home, expecting the enemy would

advance the report reached the

WINSTON N. c., Nov. IT,
The death toll in the riot here tonight
which followed efforts of a mob to
storm the city jail and lynch negro
prisoner had been increased at mid
night to five-a girl spectator. city
fireman and three negroes. The police
believe that a detailed search to-mor
row will show that at least seven per
sons and maybe more were killed.


Upward of a score of persons are be-
lieved to have been injured, five or six
Of them seriously. They are mostly
Hhite persons, and include two men,
bers of the Home Guard, which was
called out when the mob made its sec
ond visit to the Jail after shooting a
negro and accidentally wounding a
white prisoner in the afternoon.


Try to Lynch Negro


The mob was trying to lynch negro
accused of shooting j. E. Childress and
Sheriff Flint and attacking Mrs. Chill
dress last night.



on in different parts of the city, the
mob finally having broken into small
groups. Efforts Of the home guard
and the police to restore order were
unavailing even at that time and Gov
ernor Beckett was asked to intervene.
He ordered Hon.c Guards here from
Greensboro and arranged to have a
company of regular soldiers sent from
Camp Polk. near Raleigh.


The known dead are Rachael Levi, 8
Young woman bystander, who was shot
through the dungs, and Robert Young,
a fireman, who also was shot.


Negro Hurt Seriously


The mob first formed this afternoon
about $3.50 o'clock and stormed the
jail. Three shots we're fired and the
negro accused of shooting the two men
and attacking Mrs. Childress was Sc
riously wounded, while white pris-
oner named Tragg was hit in the arm
by stray bullet.


After some difficulty the police sue
ceeded in clearing the crowd out Of
the building and then the mayor called
out the home guard. Quiet reigned for
time, but later the report went
around that the negro shot was not the
man that had been sought. BY night
fall the mob had reformed and started
marching for the Jail, which was sur
rounded by home guards.


Hardware stores were broken into
and revolvers, shotguns and other
weapons and ammunition taken. AS
the mob marched it increased in size,
and when it's objective was reached it
numbered several thousand.


Fight Mob with Hose


The Mayor sought to address the
crowd, but could not be heard In the
meantime fire companies had arrived,
and when the mob broke for the Jail
the firemen turned water on them.


Firing Immediately followed and
Young was shot dead. A bullet hit
Mrs. Levi, who was watching near by.
The home guards answered the volley,
but the mob quickly overpowered them
and went into the Jail. Two members
Of the guard were badly hurt by being
thrown bodily down a stairway which
they we're guarding.


Apparently the mob did not find the
negro it sought, for no more Of the
prisoners were fired upon. After an
hour or more the mob left the Jail and
started marching through the business
section Of the town.

hrand-new fireboat Christ1ana Baird.

aboard and the Christiana Baird, Lot
yet full-fedeed .fireboat, had its
baptism Of flame. 1t was assisted by
the tug Henry jackson, equipped with
pumps.


The tide turned at about the time
into action, removing the peril from
the American Can Company's plant and
starting the blazing boats upstream
from the railroad bridge. The boats
were badly damaged The freight cars
were destroyed. The bridge was still
in commission. though several stretches
Of ties were charred. No estimate of

LONDON, June 7.--Reuter's CORE
spondent at British headquarters in
France sends the following analysis of
the situation on the Western and
Italian battle-f fronts


Between May 81 and June the
Germans made considerable progress
between Noyon and Chateau Thierry.
namely, four to five miles between
Soissons and Chateau Thierry and one
or two miles between Noyon and Sois-
sons. Their attacks on the rest Of the
salient have been local


On June ! the enemy attacked with
tanks southeast of Rheims in order to
capture high ground, but the attack
failed and the French regained the lost
ground and captured four tanks. The
Germans have hesitated to make
direct attack on Rheims, as it long
had been prepared with various fortifi-
cations. The French have barricaded
the streets and the underground de-
fences would make the city very diff
cult to capture.


Immediate Danger Over


Except for the moral effect, the
Germans would gain very little by the
capture of Rheims, unless they could
drive the French back as far as the
important railway junction on the high
ground. Since June the Germans
have made only local efforts to capture
the crossings Of the Disc, the Aisne
and the OurcQ.


"The French resistance has been
much strengthened, and they have
made important counter attacks, capt
urlng several hundred prisoners. The
enemys progress, therefore, has been
checked and the immediate danger is
over.


The German plans now are suf-
tciently clear After crossing the
Aisne River they intended to advance
as far southwark as possible, with q
defensive left flank on the Marne River
IN order to protect their thrust south
west toward Paris along the valleys of
the Disc and Ourcq.


Although the immediate danger
here is over, the situation is still seri-

divisions since May 27 A few of these
came from the groups east of the
Grown Princes army which holds the
line from the Disc to Argonne. Until
