fresh troops are to be used the situa-
tlon will remain anxious.
There are some signs that the Ger
mans intend to continue the frontal
attack between the Marne and Mont
dIdier, but these signs at present are
indefinite, and the Germans may still
hope to thrust westward toward Amiens
or other parts of the line.

The sharpest fighting continues
around the sector of Veuilly-la-

have been attacking shoulder to

were fighting in wood that cor-
tanned numerous enemy machine gun
emplacements. When this dispatch
was filed the line was uncertain. but
it was evident that progress was be-
ing accomplished by the Allied
troops.

machine gun position, killed the gun
ners and brought back the piece.


The ambulance workers courage
ously remained in the open under fire

afterward brought safely into the
American lines.

by the Allies, while the Germans
suffered the heaviest of losses.

Bascayne Bay. Sugarloaf Key, An
c!ote Keys and Key West, on the Flor


ida coast. are the principal places in
this country where experiments in
spong cultivation have been made. The
various methods are as follows: Seed
sponges are cut into small pieces and.
after having been attached by wiring
or spindle to circular or triangular
cement blocks, are dropped or lowered
depending upon the depth) to rest on
the ocean bottom, where they remain
Tor year or two, until they reach a
size proper for commercial purposes.
They are then taken by the hook when
new cuttings are attached and the
cement blocks let down again. Another
method was to string them on a wire
held horizontal by stakes driven in the
bottom. In doing this. however,
various difficulties arose. The sponges
became loose and rotated on the wire.
enlarging the hole made through them,
and destroyed the wires, until, after
many trials and experiments, a lead
wire with copper core was success
fully used.-St. Nicholas Magazine.

denburg's forces almost everywhere

Aug. 2S.-British troops today com
pleted the capture of Trones Wood,
north of the River Somme.


Canadian troops, in their advance
astride the Scarpe yesterday, captured
more than 1000 Germans.


While intermittent fighting contin-
ues virtually everywhere along the
British 'front.'. the battle begins to
show signs of slowing up.


The Germans have delivered many
counter attacks along the line, but
none of them really has gained any
thing. In virtually every case the
counter r-attacks have finally had dis
astrous results for the Germans, for

period. When re-attacked, the Ger

many casualties.

ground. Some of it had not been in

since 1914.

the moment, have had the effect of re.
tardtng operations. German resistance
this morning seems to have stiffened
considerably.

From the Atlantic.


Friends who had been and seen and
who had come home again had gone off
blitheiy and unselfshly- 80 drive ambu-
lances. to nurse the wounded, to know
the storm center for themselves: and
they had come back sobered, which was
Ineligible. and silent. which was un-
Ineligible. That they should speak
modestly of their deeds was natural, but
that they should be so strangely reticent
in speaking of the grim total fact and of
their inner reactions was unnatural.
They had been willing to communicate
a few items from their adventure. but
of their total experience they would
not speak. The cleverest raconteur
broke down. The most discerning phi
losopher found himself beyond his depth.
A touch of the ineffable seemed to have
entered into the lives of all such who
had seen and shared. however briefly
and humbly, in the strain and stress of
the storm center.

AMSTERDAM, Nov. "a (By The As
sociated Press ).-When the former
German Crown Prince arrived at the
Zuyder Zee fishing town of Enkhuyzen
Thursday he received a different vel
come from that which he encountered
elsewhere in Holland.


AS he descended from the railway
car with a staggering gait, wearing
fur coat, howls of execraton arose
from the thousands gathered outside
the station gates. The outburst of hos
tility seemed to perturb him somewhat.


The government yacht which was to
have taken the former Crown Prince
to the island of Wieringen, which will
be his future abode in Holland, ground
ed IN the fog. A little tugboat was
substituted. Affecting Indifference, the
former Crown Prince stepped up to
the gangway and lit a cigarette The
tug cast loose Immediately and disap-
peared in the fog amid the angry
shouts of the populace.


Mosterland, a hamlet consisting of
a score Of small farmsteads and fisher
mems huts on the bleak, lonely island
of Wieringen, situated some distance
from the Dutch naval station at Hell
der, is the home assigned to the in
termed former German Crown Prince.
The local pastors humble two-storied
residence has been leased furnished for
six months, and here the former Grown
Prince will live.


Village Fishermen Hostile


The house, which is without the
slightest attraction, is off the beaten
track and is hardly ever visited by
strangers. The hamlet itself is inhab-
tied for the most part by smussel fish
ermen, who, after their experiences
with Uboats during the war, view the
guests advent with anything but favor


The sole communication between the
island of Wieringen and the mainland
is small steamer which carries mail
and makes two trips daily.


To the furnishings of the parsonage,
which are very simple, there has been
added small billiard table and bath
Adjoining a Bible class room, furnish
ings have been installed for the former
/ Grown Princes guard.


A lonelier retreat for the former
/ Crown Prince could hardly be mag
ined


William Hohenzollern, the former
German Emperor, has not left the
grounds of Amerongen Castle since he
was interned there, Dutch newspapers
say.


Attends Religious Services
The former Emperor begins each day
with walk about the castle grounds
and then attends a religious service
conducted by Count Won Dentinck or
the counts son. The day closes with
another walk in the gardens. The off
GERS of his suite, however, dash about
the country in automobiles.


The pastor Of the village church
twice has dined with the former EN-
peror's party. Other local notables also
have visited the castle.


Some Dutch papers criticise the gov
ernment for placing special telephone
facilities at the disposal of the former
Emperor. The Bentinck family again
emphasizes the fact that they received
the former Emperor only at the request

BALTIMORE, Md, February 16.-The

Berlin reports an ebb in the wave
of crime that was observed there
in March. At that time the news
papers were filled with the daring
ventures of burglars and thieves
generally. Houses were broken into
right and left every night, and
some thieves even chose the daytime
for their operations An occa sional
murder accompanied their exploits.
Things finally became intolerab BILE.
and then the authorities began to
act. They had decided that one
substantial cause was the shortage
of policemen, many of the force
having been called into the army.
They remedied this by adding rein
forcements. Soldiers temporarily
exempt from military duty were
also assigned to the police force.
In this way patrolling parties of
police or soldierss secured the
streets throughout the night. The
result is that Berlin is now COM
paratively free from night robberies.

to be anything but merry. The dispo-

gloomy. The stigma of military de-
feat has been eclipsed momentarily by
political uncertainty, food stringency
and disturbed economic conditions.


Never before, even during the war,
have beggars and street venders been
met with in such numbers in Berlin.
Three years ago a soldier would not
have been permitted to walk the streets
in uniform and beg. Professional beg
gars and crippled and invalid. soldiers
multiply daily, and their numbers are
augmented by other soldiers who sell
cigarettes, soap and sweetmeats brought
in from west of the Rhine, where such
things have been more plentiful than
in Berlin. AN odd holiday spectacle is
an able-b bodied soldier in uniform
grinding out Christmas music from a
street organ.

mer Platz and Friedrichstrasse present
an incongruous appearance, with street
stalls filed with flimsy wares and sub
stitutes for Christmas pastry and wax
candles.

through trains have been withdrawn
and local trains have been stripped of
ordinary comforts, such as dining ia
cilities, heating and illumination
Trips which ordinarily took twelve
hours now take thirty. Trains are
taken off without notice, and printed
schedules are worthless. The news

cheer.

Nov. 1.-THE majority Of the American
troops got under way at 5 80 this morn

began to move earlier. In glorious. crisp.
sunshiny weather one marching column
crossed the Meuse River at stenay, NOV

toward Contains. heading toward Briey

Coming close after the first line troops

expedition better equipped than those
now moving toward Germany. The

sting. No bursting shells. no "spit-spit"

! coat and fun winter marching equip

NEW LONDON, Conn, March s.
The steel hull of the former we'll known
Fall River Line steamer Puritan is
ashore in Little Hay Harbor, Fishers
Island, seven miles from New London.
The Puritan and the Pilgrim were dis
mantled about two years ago and their
hulks have been anchored ever since
just north Of the New York Yacht Club
station.


The Puritan's cable parted shortly
after 10 o'clock this morning, when
the northwest gale was at its height,
and the once Queen of Long Island
Sound" made bee line for the Hotel
Griswold's pier, missing it by only a
few feet The old craft then made
another tack, passed Black Ledge and
Southwest Ledge Lighthouse, off the
mouth of the harbor, bowled across
Long Island Sound and astonished the
natives on the island when she majest-
ically entered Little Hay Harbor.


The Scott Wrecking Company will
send tugs to tow the Puritan back to
port tomorrow if she is in condition
to make the return trip.

"Mrs. Warren's Profession" in

Twelve yers ago the play ran one
night. Mary Shaw played then, as
now, the part of Mrs. Warren and
Arnold DAILY played Frank Gardiner.
The house was sold out within few
hours after the box office opened. and
on the first night such crowds gathered
in front of the theatre that police re-
serves had to be called to keep order.
Tickets sold for as high as twenty
five dollars, because rumor had been
circulated that the police might in
terfere and close the theatre. For
once, rumor was right. Representa-
tives of the Society for the Suppress
sion of Vice were present as we'll as
representatives of the Police Depart
ment. They claimed that the play was
a menace to. public morals, and their
claim was upheld by the courts. The
next night the theatre was dark.

ers decided to revive the play there
were many to predict that once again

opening night at the Comedy Theatre

resentatives there. But this time there

morality. The times had marched.

There were no trenches. 1t was open
warfare. Except sor the scant cover
Of walls. trees and bitches the troops
were exposed. Even the woods offered
no concealment from above for the
leaves were just bursting into bud. The
allies called upon aviation for help
Orders were given to harry the advance
ing columns in every possible manner
10 as to cause confusion and give the
allied achievements time to arrive.


Mission Admirably Fulfilled.


This mission was admirably fulfilled.
Not only was the German morale
shaken by the repeated attacks day and
night, giving the tired troops no rest,
but the losses inflicted were severe. In
other words. il is perhaps no exaggera-
ton to say that the aviatorS helped
considerably to save the situation. The
allied nocturnal bombarding groups
were active from the first night or the
offensive, but it was only after the
that the daylight bombing saus drons

Having no more German planes to
fight the great combat groups, which
had just won decisive air victory,
were loosed like a swarm OF hornets
inside the enemy's lines with orders to
use their machine guns on everything
moving on the roads. The attacks were
carefully organized. Each squadron or
patrol had a special mission. the guild
ing idea being always to strike hardest
where the enemy's movement was the
most dangerous. French fighters. hav-
ing reached the particular strip OF road
assigned to them, would fly high like
hawks sailing back and forth. watching
for signs of life. The moment con-
voy appeared or column Of troops

tree tops, raking the easy target with
machine guns. causing horses 20 run

guns swooped down rapidly. one after
another. the motors roaring and the

pleteiy. Others took fright and. de-
spite the efforts of their riders to con-

fields. dragging the caissons and wag-
ons after them. Within a few seconds
the entire column was dispersed and

men and horses and the wreckage of

ITO Wilde, new come from Oxford, the


life Of London seemed barbaric,
splendid with the mystery of the
East. The city wore the expression of
beautiful and silent sphinx crouching
upon Chinese mat, with eyes Of satin
trimmed with gold. Her counterpart,
hewn out Of marble, with name of
amethyst, sat in the corner of his room
upon the mantel, inviolate and immobile
She watched his every move, tormented
him with silent scrutiny, threatened with
pains of hell. He feared to meet her
gaze, babe her BECOME. Her lovers, the
dog faced Anubis, gaunt Memnon, Nilus
with his broken arm, were not dead. Let
her away to Egypt; they waited her, gods
of an elder day. They were not dead
"Only one God has ever died"


There is every reason for believing
Wilde spoke the truth, though poets
weep for Pan, who is no more and vir-
gins seated meath the myrtle mourn
Apollo and Pierrot cries in vain to his lost
Diana


And yet, if all these ancient gods are
dead, Hermes and Mars and Cupid, they
died young nor ever knew decay. youth"
said La Rochefoucauld, sis a fever Of the
soul" Their hearts were aname with the
stuff of Immortality. They passed, we
know-whitherf who nowsf-and with
them went much Of the beauty and charm
Of Greece and Rome out of the world
They passed, for when men cease to wor-
ship at his shrine god must die-a god
unknown cannot exist, his life being spent
in the human heart, feeding upon the
prayers hidden there, nurtured like a babe
in the womb. They passed like little chill
dren to be born again far from the bias
phemy that had destroyed their power,
soiled their loveliness. With heads bowed,
faces averted, they went to seek a new
heaven and new earth-hope being the
chiefest attribute of gods


But because they were so young when
they went away we still refuse to believe
them dead. How could such strong and
vivid creatures, so much that is everlast-
ing, be murdered by weaklings no more
cruel than our fathers fathersf 1t seems
impossible-and Yet the gods of yesterday
are now no more.

The Grand Duchy of Luxembourg is
ruled by the Grand Duchess Marie
Adelaide. who is the youngest sovereign
In all Europe. She was crowned on her
eighteenth birthday in 1912. The father
of the present ruler was Grand Duke
William Alexander, a descendant Of
William of Orange. She was but thir-
teen years old when her father died.
Her mother. the Grand Duchess Marie
Anne. Portuguese Pripcess Of the house
of Braganza, ruled as regent until her
daughter was crowned.


The young Grand Duchess flashed
into the spotlight in August. 1914. when
she Indignantly refused the Kaiser's de-
mand that his armies be permitted to
cross her little kingdom. The refusal
did her little good. however, for the
soldiers tramped across her little do
main and into her palace Ever since
the Grand Duchess virtually has been a
prisoner with Prussian guards around
her palace.

ish patrol boat observed a submarine
half a mile distant, apparently re-

ordered full speed in the direction OK

ming her before she was able to sub

med an enemy submarine. The Brit

plates and remained imbedded. Both
craft endeavored to extricate them
selves. The enemy, through using his
ballast tanks. almost came to the sur
face, bringing the British submarine
along. Then the German drew away
in great difficulty, apparently frantic
ally endeavoring to keep afoat, but

WITH THE BRITISH ARMY IN
FRANCE, April II. I0:00 a. mo-
The desperate efforts by great forces
of the enemy yesterday afternoon and
last night to exploit his successes about
Bailleul and Wytschaete met with
costly failure.


The battle west of Bailleul has been
continuous and sanguinary. Time at
ter time the enemy forces flung them
selves against the defenders in intense
assaults, but on each occasion the
British troops held their own and
threw the onrushing Germans back
with huge losses.


A tremendous artillery duel is rag
ing alone the Northern front. Through
out the night thousands of guns of all
calibres made the war zone hideous
with their mighty detonations. There
was no cessation of this protracted
fencing between the heavy batteries,
and this morning the contest was still
continuing, the vibration shaking win
dows forty and fifty miles away.


In the extreme north numerous
enemy attacks during the afternoon
and evening followed the capture by
the Germans of Wytschaete and Span
broekmolen. Later in the afternoon
the battle swung further northward
and the Germans attempted an advance
The attempt was q complete failure,
and great numbers of the attacking
infantry were shot down at short range
by machine gun and rifle fire.


The German centre in this assault
appeared to suffer heavily as the waves
came forward. and the f1anks, in at
tempting a withdrawal, came under a
grillino fire, which left the ground
strewn with dead and wounded.


Hail of Death Sweeps Foe,


About Wyschaete the grim struggle
continued, the British not only hold
ing their own but putting all their
power in an effort to push the enemy
back from the town, and last evening
the British reported entering the place.


Shortly after noon the Germans de-
livered an attack against the Damn
strasse line, between Hollebeke and
subsequent enemy concentration in this
region was dispersed by the artillery.


The continuous enemy attacks all
the afternoon southwest of Bailleul
were without exception repulsed with
heavy losses. The German artillery
filled the area west of the stricken
town with gas and high explosive shells
as an adjunct to the infantry attack.
At dusk the enemy drove forward again
and made a vicious thrust at the Brit
ish lines.


The advancing troops pushed through
the hail of death. but soon wavered and

ALBANr. Sept. e.--The dollar gas law
operative in Albany for the last ten
years was declared unconstitutional to-
day by Supreme Court Justice Has
brouck. The decision vitality affects
similar statutes effective in parts Of
New York city.


Justice Hasbrouck's decision enjoins
the upstate Public Service Commission
the Attorney-General and the District
Attorney of Albany county from enforc-
Ing the dollar rate for gas distributed
after September %. when the Municipal
Gas Company's new tariff of $3.50 a
thousand cubic feet becomes effective.

OF 1907 fixing the minimum rate at 81
was constitutional for ten years, the
recent increase in the cost of labor and
the price of materials renders its en-
forcement confiscatory, negotiable and
unconstitutional. An immediate appeal
will bring the case before the Appellate
Division at Saratoga next week.

James Mackey, thirteen years Old, and
his little brother John, eleven, after
receiving their report cards from
school on Wednesday, put their heads
together and decided that they would
run away rather than face the dis
pleasure of their parents at such low
marks.


The boys were brought to police
headquarters here to-day and telc-
phone messages were sent to their
father. John Mackey. of 2069 Ryer Ave
nue., TIE Bronx. They had with them
a suitcase containing two Boy Sconr
uniforms, the two report cards that
had caused the trouble, their savings
bank books and revolver which they
said belonged to their uncle, who is a
policeman.


They told the police that they re.
ccived weekly allowance of 25 cents
from their mother, and that they had
saved it so they had enough to start
their trip. When they began their
journey Wednesday morning they rode
by trolley to Pelham and then walked
the fifteen miles to Port Chester, N. Y.


After their hike they rested by at
tending a vaudeville show, and then
found an outbuilding, where they slept
They were caught this morning four
miles further on their travels, as they
were trudging along the railroad tracks
at Cos Cob, Conn. Residents telephoned
to the police here, and the weary
youngsters were brought in.

Scenes greeting troops upon recap
tured ground amply illustrate the ef-

and machine guns. German bodies
are found everywhere.

mass attacks. French troops here
ran the risk of being encircled

withdrew, and, at the same moment,

LONDON. Aug. 25.--In the last two
days the British third and fourth
armies have bagged 10000 prisoners.
among them being six battalion com

brigade adjutant general. The adju-
tant general tried to escape on horse
back, but was taken when his mount
vas shot from under him.


The British troops are thrilled with
their Srogress now. They are re
claiming ground, every foot Of which
is hallowed territory. The sacrifices
of comrades in earlier days on this
very ground is not forgotten. Every
village that is retaken is a shrine
where gallant British soldiers died in
days gone by.


This ground, where the British are
pushing ahead is honeycombed with old
duGouts and trenches. New trenches
have been dug in among the old ones
until the ground is fairly covered
with them. The field is one OF the
grimmest. most deSolate spots on the
western front.


II was in the light Of fun harvest
moon carly Friday morning that Eng
lish and Scottish battalions stormed
the villages Of Gomiecourt. Ervillers.
Hamelincourt, Boyelles, and Boiry-
Becqucrelle. The troops that took
Gomiecourt discovered the Germans
massing for a counter attack. The
enemy evidently believed there had
been reached their objective and
would not attempt to attack further.
They were quickly disillusioned.


The British broke up their counter
attack, took 500 prisoners and killed
many. The British troops quickly
carried their line east of these viii

The Germans yesterday began their
fourth great offensive of the year.
After short but terrific lombard
ment, they stormed forward on a
twenty-one-mile front between
Montdidier and Noyon, along the
southern side of the Picardy sa-
lient and adjoining the new
Champagne salient.


Despite the severe losses inflicted
on them by the French, Crown
Prince Rupprecht's men pushed
forward to depth of two and a
half miles at certain points and
at one point four miles.


On the wings of the new salient, the
French broke the force of the
blow, preventing the enemy from
advancing far. The Germans
progressed more than a mile near
the western end of the front at
tackled, capturing the towns of
Rubescourt, LIE Fretoy and
Mortemer. On the right the enc
my made only slight gains against
the desperate Allied resistance
before Connecancourt and Vile.
In the centre of the line Luden-
dorf's troops were subjected to
a murderous fire, but by sheer
weight forced the French back to
the region of Ressons-sur- Matz,
the point of the maximum with
drawal.


The enemy's attack is continuing
violently, General Foch reported
last night. Along the whole front
the French were resisting stub
bornly, exacting tremendous sac
rifices from the Germans for
every foot of ground yielded.
BY this blow, predicted by observ-
ers since the thrust toward the
Marne two weeks ago, the Ger
mans probably intend to get
astride the Disc River, beat in the
Allied salient between the Picar-
dy and Champagne fronts, and
then sweep toward Paris, with the
Disc protecting their right flank.
The American positions in the Mont
didier sector were violently ham,
mered by the enemy's guns. but
no infantry action developed.
These positions adjoin to the
west the front attacked.


In the Champagne salient the French
made minor advances, gaining
ground east of Hautebraye, north
west Of Scissors, improving their
positions east Of Chevy, south of
the Ourcq, and advancing farther
near Eloup and Bussiares, north
west Of Chateau Thierry. Ameri-
can troops are holding parts Of
the front near Bussiares.

northwest Of Chateau Thierrv

heavy losses.

London. Jan. 30.-Enerseically
following up their victorious action
on the Asiaso plateau of Sunday
and Monday. the Italians yesterday
won even more importa~' successes
on both sides Of the Frenzela Val
ley. Three dominating heights
Col del Rosso. Col Dechele and
Monte di Val Bella-were stormed
and held against furious counter at
tacks. The Italian bag Of prisoners
was increased to $500. and six
cannon and 100 machine guns
were captured. the Rome war office
announced today.


Austrian Losses stagger.


The losses of the Austrfans are
reported to have been staggering.
Two OF their divisions were almost
completely wiped out. Hundreds
fell before the bayonets of the Ital-
ians In futile reactions on Rosso
Hill and Monte di Val Bella The
loss of the three heights Is consid-
cred by the German war office to-
night, but the statement declares
that all Italian attacks in the re-
sion of Monte Sisemol broke down
with. severe losses. The Austrians
exposed the new italian positions to
a delue of shell all day long. but
without shaking the hold of Gen.
Diaz's troops, who retaliated BY
bombarding the entrenchment be-
hind the enemy's lines.


Salient ObIIterated.


The Italian success, which IS
even more important than that Of
the French in the Monte Tomba sec
tor earIier in the month, complete
~ obliterates the salient which the
invaders had driven into the front
between Asiago and the Brenta
River and which offered the most
accessible routo-down the 'Frenzela
Valley to the edge of the Venetian
lpi2iu. The Austrian army under
Field Marshal Conrad captured
those positions on December % last,
Just as their prolonged offensive
vas reaching the limit of its ex-
tension, so that they succeeded I'm
holding them little more than a
month.


Their loss constitutes a vital blow
to Austrian hopes OF reaching the
plains easily and quickly with the
opening of spring operations By
their two mid-winter Offensives the
French and the Italians have re-
moved the greatest menace to the
safety Of the Italian defensive lines
between the Piaye and the Brenta
and between the Brenta and the
AsiagO plateau and therefore vastly
bettered the chances of Italy's re-
pelling the invader for good and all
when the next attempt is launched.


RnEds on West Front.


Raiding thrusts by both sides con-
tinued on the West front yesterday,
but the infantry fighting was some
what obscured by the intense activity
Of the opposing aerial forces. Both
on Monday and yesterday the British
slrmen carried out extensive opera
tions, bombing enemy detectives at
Roulers, Menin, Tournai and other
places. Thousands of rounds were
fired at enemy troops from British
machines both during. the daytime and
at night.


On Monday the British flyers
brought down eight machines and lost
three themselves. Yesterday five
more German planes were shot down
in battle with French aviators.

JUAREZ, Mexico, March 30.-Fran-
cisco Villa continues to play his fo1-
like tricks on the Mexican federal
troops as he did when he was "Pancho"
Villa. the bandit, and rode the Sierra
Madre mountains of western Chihua-
hua like a Mexican Robin Hood.


American mining men who had run
the gantlet of Villas lines and reached
the border here on a passenger train,
the windows of which had been shot
out by Villas men. told the first con-
nected story Of Villas operations
around CanutilIo. Durango. just over
the chihuahua state line, against the
federal column which pursued him
from Jiminez with its 100 mounted dare
devils.


After the fight at Laguna de Esta-
cada. Chihuahua, Villa led his men
southwest toward the Rio F1oT1oo'
where he had hidden while Gen. Per-
shing was pursuing him. There are
rido, where Villa likes to battle and
soak the rheumatism and saddle sore
ness out of his limbs after hard
campaign But before he could enjoy
his private baths in the Durango river
Gen. Eduardo Hernandez and Gen.
Francisco Gonzales closed in on him
with two cavalry columns.


Only Pretended Flight.


Pretending to flee before these ad-
vancing columns, Villa and his men
dashed through the little mountain
town of Canutillo. with the federal
cavalrymen pursuing them a few hours
later. Villas little army disappeared
over the ridge of sand hill with the
evening sun. The federals went Into
Iy,%$ III q tNr
intending to resume the pursuit at
daybreak It was a moonlight night.
and few sentries were posted. a custom
not uncommon in Mexico.


halted behind the first. ridge. had all Of
his men leave their hats in a pile. wheeled
his column and rode back toward Canu-
tillo Scouts reported the location Of the
light Whispered orders were given that
no one but those wearing hats should be
fired upon. The attack then began With
a warhoop which was as terrifying as
the famous rebel yell, the Villa column
swept down upon the camp. shooting from
the saddle at every man who could be
seen In the confusion which followed
the surprise night attack the federal SOL
taking them for Villas men. After sharp
encounter Villa rode through Canutillo
once more. leaving small detachment
there to hold the town against the federals.


Used Populace in Deception.


There, again, he played another one of
his old tricks. He had these men hide in
the adobe houses. where they cut loop
holes facing the side from which the fed
eral attack was expected. These Villa
men also made all Of the civilians crowd
into these houses and give vivas for Villa
to make the enemy believe the Villa force
was many times larger than it really was
The small Villa band succeeded in holding
off the federals until Villa could lead his
main column In circle and strike the
federal column from the rear. Again the
government troops were slaughtered, the
mining man said. and many were made
prisoners and later executed.


These are only two of Villas bag of
tricks. Another favorite one is to send
his men against the enemy, then have
them retire in apparent disorder until
they reach canyon or other place
easily fortified by Villa The pursuers
are led into this trap and they are sub
jected to a. sweeping fire from the
rocks and are usually annihiliated.
This piece of native strategy was used
against the federals at San Andres,
Chihuahua; again at Rosario. Durango.
and at Pederanales, Chihuahua.


Carries Telegraph Operator.


Villa has frequently forced federal
telegraph operators to send misleading
messages directing troop trains to pro-
ceed to a point where a trap was laid
for them. This was done at Laguna,
Chihuahua, and paymaster general
and all Of his guard were killed.

FRANCE, Sept. 6.-Five Americans
have been decorated with British hon

on the British front. They are:


Lieutenant Allan Francis Bonnalie,
of San Francisco, and Lieutenant
Glenn D. Ransom, of Grand Rapids,
Mich; Corporal John Johnston and
Privates Lawrence Bartley Collier and
Robert Hurley Hall.

Conduct medal, and military medals

and Private Hall.


Went to Comrades Aid


Lieutenant Bonnalie on August 13
led two other airplanes on a long pho
tographic reconnaissance right near
Bruges, Belgium. While over Thourout
all three machines were attacked, but
they succeeded in taking the required
photographs.


The three Allied airplanes then
started back, but met six Fokkers,
which dived to attack. While heavily
engaged himself, Lieutenant Bonnalie
observed that one Of his machines was
in difficulties.


Lieutenant Bonnalie broke off his
combat and dived to the assistance of
his comrade. His enemy, taking ad
vantage of this, attacked from the
rear; but as the bullets were ripping
through his machine the lieutenant
drove off the enemy from the tail of
the crippled British plane.
Meanwhile Lieutenant Bonnalie's
elevator control shot through and
half of the machines tail was shot
away. in consequence of which the air.
plane began to sideslip. The lieuten-
ant kept his machine facing the British
line by ruGder control, his observer
continuing to fight the attacking air
craft from the rear gun mounting, and
succeeded eventually in driving off the
enemy.


With this gallant assistance Lieuten-
ant Bonnalie managed to cross the
British lines at a low altitude and
landed without fatal results.


Cared for Wounded Under Fire
Lieutenant Glenn D. Ransom won his
military cross at Merckham. He is
medical officer attached to British
battalion and worked continuously
under fire in caring for the men of his
own and other battalions and also
wounded Germans.

August 12, was in the line opposite
Boyelles in charge of a post The

General Foch struck two great
counter blows yesterday.


The first drove the Germans back
two miles in the centre of the
new salient, where they had
reached the Aronde River. The
second, struck in full force
against the west wing Of the sa-
lent, pushed the enemy back over
a seven and a half mile front.
IN their second blow the poilus
gained more than a mile of ter
ritory between Montdidier and
st. Maur, retook the village of
Belloy and the heights east of
Courcelles and captured more
than thousand prisoners.
The Germans, meanwhile, continued
their violent assaults all along the
line, between Noyon and Mont
didier. They succeeded in push
ing forward nearly. four miles on
the east side of the salient. On
the west side the brilliant de-
fence of the French held them
back.


Despite the murderous fire of the
Allied guns, Ludendorff poured
new divisions into the great drive.
attempting to crush all resistance
and smash the Allied salient
stretching into the German line
toward Noyon.


All observers report the tremendous
losses inflicted on the attacking
masses, which came on in unend-
ing numbers. The French with
drew slowly from their positions
on their right, exacting heavy toll
for every vantage point relin-
quished.


The American forces northwest of
Chateau Thierry launched new
attack at the German lines, taking
Belleau Wood in desperate fight
ing, the Paris War Office reported
last night. Earlier in the day.
cooperating with the French, Per-
shing's men again pushed for
ward, capturing prisoners and
booty and infiicting heavy losses.
Australians on the front before
Amiens, pursuing their earlier
successes there, advanced more
than half a mile on a one and a
half mile front into the German
lines, capturing nearly three hun
dred prisoners and a considerable
quantity of war materials.
Berlin claimed the capture of 10. 900
additional prisoners, bringing
the total to $4,000 for three days
of the new drive. The German
War Office also reported the re-
pulse of desperate Allied counter
attacks southwest of Noyon and
near Chateau Thierry.

LONDON, July 2.--The British Of
fetal press correspondent with the
British army in Mesopotamia sends
the following dispatch:


"The Turk has been dissipated on
all three fronts during the past year.
Meanwhile peace has reigned in the
city Of Bagdad and the amenities Of
life have been multiplying for the
army and for the civil population.


"Bagdad was dead to all appearances
when the British army entered on
March IL last year. Now it is a bus
Ting hive of humanity. Thousands of
workmen pass through the streets early
and late. The main street is paved and
lighted. There is a constant stream of
traffic and the sleepiest old women
who haunt the streets have become
adept at lodging the American motor
cars which run through the streets.


"A police force and fire depart
ment have been organized. The old
fashioned oil lamps in the streets
have been replaced by electric lights.
The water supply has been improved
and extended. Mosques have been re-
| paired, roads have been paved and
schools, included a training school for
| native teachers, have been opened.


"The streets now are we'll watered
in dry weather and sanitary officials
have penetrated che most hidden
corners of the city. The municipal
government has been made self-sup.
porting. Two bridges have been
thrown across the Tigrs River. These
are some of the changes which have
come with British occupation, ane
| have come quietly and unnoticed."

Why are mineral waters harmful? Are

Laxative mineral waters are harmful,
because they irritate the mucous mem
brane and in time produce intestinal
catarrh. They also expose the liver and
kidneys to the harmful effects of over
work. Mineral waters are no more nat
ural healing agencies than are minerals
themselves. No one would think of rec
ommendinG iron pyrites or limestone as
a healing agent; neither arc the great
salt beds or alkali deposits regarded as
natural healing agents. Mineral waters
are simply rain water which has been
contaminated by coming in contact with
various mineral substances while per-
colating through the earth.


Mineral waters are in no way benc-
fetal to healthy man. They may. in
some instances, prove of temporary serv-
Ice In emergencies, but their constant
use Is now recognized as being highly
detrimental. Many European physicians
who formerly recommended mineral wa
ters very freely to their patients now
condemn their use for the reasons above
stated.

ters which are remarkable for their eX-
treme purity or freedom from both min
eral contamination and germs or bac-

A call has been sent forth from the
Civil Service Commission to people liv-
ing in Washington or within committing
distance Of the city to apply for posi-
tions in the government service, as a
means Of iessening the demand for hous-
ing facilities. Congress has set aside
for the period of the war the regula-
tions requiring applicants for govern
mcnt posts to be examined in the
states or territories in which they reside.
This virtually valves the apportionment
rule, which has been bane to the de-
pertmental service for many years. Had
the waiver been immediate and full
many Of the troubles experienced by the
government since the war began would
have been averted So fixed is the idea
that a Nashingtonian is barred from
the government service that many who
were fully competent did not seek ap-
pointments, while the government was
securing the states for workers. Age lin
its should be waived as we'll as residen-

To THE EDITOR OF THE SUN--Sir: Once

called Usona. Its people had their
farms and flour mills. their spinning
wheels and looms. flocks, woods, gold,

One day an argosy laden with gold cast

nauts too wanted these things and paid
twice over what the rich had paid, They
bought more and more the while plant

which they paid.


They were all -ich and prosperous,

ing out, their roofs getting leaky, their

But. captain bold, a:e there no other

I'VE passed many OF them, some

they did not need to come SO far as your

at Inglaterra. some at Erin, some at

You will guess half f-dozen nationali-
ties as their eighty-six bronzed faces
come up the street. Their features,
taches are as varied as the races of
man. Only when the colors float by is
there explanation. There is only one
Tricolor these days - and only one For
eign Legion. AS you clutch your hat
from your head and the thrill of gleam-
ing bayonets and tramping heroes
sweeps over you, there comes new
sense of the cause for which the civil
lized world is fighting, fresh realiza-
ton of the banded strength of the Allies
who would slay the enemy of all that is
beautiful and free and just.


Much has been written of the Foreign
Legion, but the tale of their heroism
is unending. Service stripes and wound
stripes the eighty-six show without num-
ber. Each man has his decoration
From the start of the war these men
from all the world have fought and
fought and fought, without giving or
seeking quarter, without knowing re-
treat. Their unit has been cited again
and again. Their losses have been ter
rible And they have gone on fighting,
with fresh recruits, with undimnished
valor.


Like the first British army of Old Con-
temptibles, like our first American
doughboys, the Foreign Legionares
were more than fighting force, more
than mere numbers. They were fore
runners, a light upon the hills that told
France even in her darkest hour that
help would yet come. What these few
valiant souls felt in the first days of the
war, all of us, the whole civilized world,
have now come to know. The battle of
civilization that France fought and
snatched from defeat at the Marne four
years ago has become crusade to-day.
Valiant nations the world around are
following where these valiant souls led.

Americans. The Germans tonight are
in retreat beyond the Freya positions.


The Germans have retired so rapidly
at some points that the Americans have
experienced difficulty in maintaining
contact with the enemy.


More than sixty cannon, scores of
IT'S, dozens of 1908, numerous howit-
zers of various calibres and hundreds
Of machine guns were captured by the
Americans during the advance of Fri
day and Saturday. Vast quantities of
ammunition and war material of all
kinds Fell into their hands.


General Pcrshing's forces west Of
the Meuse this afternoon captured
Fosse. This represents an advance of
four miles from the starting line
through Bayonville.


The Germans gave little if any indi-
cation Of an impending retreat until
this afternoon. All morning long the
Americans on every part of the front
had met with stubborn resistance.


The opposition was especially de-
termined on the left and right, and the
American centre had pushed forward
considerably further than had either
wing. Though the centre had intended
to continue and to attain its days OBJ
jectives, it was apparent there soon
would have to be a pause if the troops
were not to be fanked.


Good News Doubted


SO certain were the military COM
manders that the Germans would not
break that the chief Of staff of the
troops in the centre belittled the re-
port arriving about 2 o'clock this after
noon that the town Of Fosse had been
taken.


One hour later, however, reports be-
gan to come thick and fast. The first
showed that resistance against the
American left had unaccountably
ceased. Then came reports indicating
that the right wing was moving ahead
at marvellous speed.


This morning, despite the increased
volume Of the enemy fire, the Ameri-
cans were steadily advancing, although
more slowly than on Friday. The line
at noon showed no losses of territory,
while some improvement of it had been
effected


Resistance Grows Weak


The first intimation that the enemy
was retreating came from the Fourth
French Army, which was advancing to
the northeast. Within a short time va
rious American units from all parts Of
the line announced that they also were
advancing and were finding the resist
ance, which was so marked all morn
ing, melting away on the right. Even
troops in motor trucks had not been
able to catch up with the enemy.


The Americans were not slow in fol-
lowing the advantage on the left wing,
which had met with the most serious
resistance, and began to press forward
imme diately in the Bois des Loges on
the heels Of the Germans, cleaning up
all who Jagged behind They pushed
their line northward for nearly mile.
Champigneville, strong point in the
Freya defence line, had been taken
earlier in the day, and the troops who
had rushed it pressed forward and
swept through Verpel, after partly sur
rounding the town.


In Rain and Mud


Through rain and mud the Americans
advanced toward Thenorgues, a mile
and half north of Verpel. The enemy
had been expected to hold there, fol
it was strong position, but very little
resistance was met with when the vii.
lage was entered.


Troops further to the right continued
their victorious march and fought thei,
way beyond Buzancy to Fosse, a strone
poitn nearly seven miles beyong yes
terday's starting point and two and s
half miles north Of Bayonville.


Bayonville is an important strategic
point, known as the heart of the Frevs
Stellung. With it's capture the Ameri
can troops had broken the Germans
| last organized defences.

battle front by Captain Archibald
Roosevelt. The soldiers came from the

taken into the trophy room, where the
many curios were explained. After
wards tea was served to the boys, who
when they left gave the former Presi-
dent cheer and said they had had the
time of their lives.

pleased to-day when he received q
cable message from France, saying that
his oldest son, Major Theodore. had
been promoted to Lieutenant Colonel,

tails of the promotion.
